whether the determination of the appeal against the interlocutory decision may—
render the trial unnecessary; or
substantially reduce the time required for the trial; or
resolve an issue of law, evidence or procedure that is necessary for the proper conduct of the trial; or
reduce the likelihood of a successful appeal against conviction in the event that the accused is convicted at trial; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.
The Court of Appeal must not give leave to appeal after the trial has commenced, unless the reasons for doing so clearly outweigh any disruption to the trial.
If the Court of Appeal refuses leave to appeal under this section, the refusal does not preclude any other appeal on the issue that was the subject of the proposed appeal.
An interlocutory appeal under section 295 is commenced by filing a notice of application for leave to appeal in accordance with the rules of court—

subject to paragraph (b), if the trial has not commenced when the interlocutory decision is made, within 10 days after the day on which the interlocutory decision is made or any extension of that period granted under section 313; or

if the trial commences within 10 days after the day on which the interlocutory decision is made, within 2 days after the day on which the trial commences or any extension of that period granted under section 313; or
if the trial has commenced when the interlocutory decision is made, within 2 days after the day on which the interlocutory decision is made or any extension of that period granted under section 313.

A copy of the notice of application for leave to appeal must be served on the respondent in accordance with section 392 or 394, as the case requires, within the relevant period specified in subsection (1) for filing the notice.

nodes.heading: Adjournment of trial if leave to appeal given
nodes.text: If the Court of Appeal gives leave to appeal against an interlocutory decision after the trial has commenced, the trial judge must adjourn the trial without discharging the jury, if reasonably practicable, until the appeal has been determined.

An appeal against an interlocutory decision is to be determined on the evidence, if any, given in the proceeding to which the appeal relates, unless the Court of Appeal gives leave to adduce additional evidence.
On an appeal under section 295, other than an appeal against a determination that the presumption against criminal responsibility is rebutted, the Court of Appeal—
may affirm or set aside the interlocutory decision; and
if it sets aside the interlocutory decision—
may make any other decision that the Court of Appeal considers ought to have been made; or
remit the matter to the court which made the interlocutory decision for determination.
If the Court of Appeal remits a matter under subsection (2)(b)(ii)—
it may give directions concerning the basis on which the matter is to be determined; and
the court to which the matter is remitted must hear and determine the matter in accordance with the directions, if any.

nodes.heading: Determination of appeal—interlocutory decision on presumption against criminal responsibility

nodes.text: This section applies to an appeal under section 295 against an interlocutory decision that the presumption against criminal responsibility has been rebutted in respect of a charge for an offence allegedly committed by a person at 12 or 13 years of age.
The appeal is to be determined on the evidence, if any, given in the proceeding to which the appeal relates, unless the Court of Appeal gives leave to adduce additional evidence.
Despite section 300(2), the Court of Appeal—
may affirm the decision that the presumption against criminal responsibility is rebutted; or
may set aside the decision and enter a judgment of acquittal of the relevant offence.

On affirming a decision that the presumption against criminal responsibility is rebutted, the Court of Appeal may order that the matter proceed to trial or to the determination of other pre-trial issues (as the case requires).
A judgment of acquittal of the relevant offence under subsection (3)(b)—
has the same effect as if it were a verdict of not guilty by the jury on the trial of the accused for the charge for the offence; and
is to be entered on the record of the court that made the decision as a decision of not guilty.

nodes.heading: Determination of interlocutory appeal to be entered on record
nodes.text: The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court must transmit the decision of the Court of Appeal to the court which made the interlocutory decision and that court must enter the decision on the court record.

nodes.heading: Case stated for Court of Appeal

nodes.text: This section applies to a proceeding in the County Court or the Trial Division of the Supreme Court for the prosecution of an indictable offence.

In a proceeding referred to in subsection (1), if a question of law arises before or during the trial, the court may reserve the question for determination by the Court of Appeal if the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so, having regard to—
the extent of any disruption or delay to the trial process that may arise if the question of law is reserved; and
whether the determination of the question of law may—
render the trial unnecessary; or
substantially reduce the time required for the trial; or
resolve a novel question of law that is necessary for the proper conduct of the trial; or
reduce the likelihood of a successful appeal against conviction in the event that the accused is convicted at trial.
The court must not reserve a question of law after the trial has commenced, unless the reasons for doing so clearly outweigh any disruption to the trial.

Section 33 of the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 also provides for the referral to the Supreme Court of questions of law that relate to the application of the Charter or the interpretation of a statutory provision in accordance with the Charter.

nodes.heading: Reservation of question of law on appeal to County Court
nodes.text: If on the hearing of an appeal under Part 6.1 to the County Court from the Magistrates' Court a question of law arises, the County Court may reserve the question for determination by the Court of Appeal if the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so, having regard to—
the extent of any disruption or delay to the hearing that may arise if the question of law is reserved; and
whether the determination of the question of law may—
render the hearing unnecessary; or
substantially reduce the time required for the hearing; or
resolve a novel question of law that is necessary for the proper conduct of the hearing.

nodes.heading: Adjournment if question of law reserved

history.raw: S. 303 amended by No. 48/2012 s. 19 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: If a court reserves a question of law under section 302 after the trial has commenced, the court must adjourn the trial without discharging the jury, if reasonably practicable, until the question of law has been determined.
If a court reserves a question of law under section 302A, the court must adjourn the hearing, if reasonably practicable, until the question of law has been determined.

nodes.heading: Refusal to reserve question of law

nodes.text: If the Supreme Court or the County Court refuses an application under section 302 or 302A to reserve a question of law, the applicant may apply to the Court of Appeal for an order calling on—
the court which dismissed the application; and
the respondent—
to show cause why the question of law should not be reserved for determination by the Court of Appeal.
On an application under subsection (1), the Court of Appeal may order that the question of law be reserved for its determination or refuse the application with or without costs.
If the Court of Appeal orders that the question of law be reserved, the court to which the order is directed must reserve the question for determination by the Court of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Case to be stated if question of law reserved

nodes.text: If a court reserves a question of law under section 302, 302A or 304, it must state a case, setting out the question and the circumstances in which the question has arisen.
The court must sign the case stated and transmit it within a reasonable time to the Court of Appeal.
The Court of Appeal may return a case stated transmitted to it under subsection (2) for amendment and the court that stated the case must amend it as required.

nodes.heading: General powers of Court of Appeal on case stated

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal may hear and finally determine a question of law set out in a case stated.

In the case of a question of law reserved under section 302, 302A or 304, the Court of Appeal may remit the question and the determination of the Court of Appeal back to the court which reserved the question.
The applicant is not required to attend the hearing under subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Judgment to be entered on record
nodes.text: The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court must transmit the judgment and order (if any) of the Court of Appeal to the court that reserved the question of law and that court must enter the judgment and order (if any) on the court record.

nodes.heading: DPP may refer point of law to Court of Appeal

nodes.text: If a person is acquitted in respect of all or any charges—
in a trial on indictment before the Supreme Court or the County Court; or
on an appeal to the County Court from the Magistrates' Court or, if the Magistrates' Court was constituted by the Chief Magistrate who is a dual commission holder, to the Court of Appeal—
the DPP may refer to the Court of Appeal any point of law that has arisen in the proceeding.

For the avoidance of doubt, if a point of law arises in an appeal proceeding, and that appeal is from the Magistrates' Court constituted by the Chief Magistrate who is a dual commission holder, subsection (1)(b) does not apply.
The Court of Appeal is to consider a point of law referred to it under subsection (1) and give its opinion on it.
An acquitted person who appears in court in person or by a legal practitioner is entitled to reasonable costs as settled by the Costs Court.
A reference under this section does not affect the trial or hearing in relation to which the reference is made or an acquittal in that trial or hearing.

nodes.heading: Status of sentences and orders during appeal period
Sentence not stayed during appeal period

nodes.text: A sentence is not stayed during the appeal period unless—
this Act or any other Act otherwise provides; or
an order is made under subsection (2).
The trial judge or, if a notice of appeal or notice of application for leave to appeal is filed, the Court of Appeal may stay a sentence if satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
See the definition of sentence in section 3.
A prisoner within the meaning of the Corrections Act 1986 who appeals, or applies for leave to appeal, to the Court of Appeal may apply to the Court of Appeal to be granted bail.
On an application under subsection (1), the Court of Appeal may grant the prisoner bail pending the appeal.
See section 323 for bail following appeal.

nodes.heading: Stay of certain orders during appeal period

nodes.text: This section applies to an order under section 84, 85B or 86 of the Sentencing Act 1991 made by the Supreme Court or the County Court.
See section 83G(1) of the Sentencing Act 1991 in relation to superannuation orders.
Unless the Supreme Court or the County Court otherwise directs, an order referred to in subsection (1) is stayed during the appeal period.
If an order is stayed under subsection (2) and the conviction is set aside on appeal, the order does not take effect unless the Court of Appeal otherwise orders.
The Court of Appeal may set aside or vary an order made by the Supreme Court or the County Court under subsection (2).
Rules of court may provide for securing the safe custody during the appeal period of any property the subject of an order referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Execution of order for forfeiture or destruction of property

nodes.text: If a court orders the forfeiture or destruction of any property in relation to an offence, the property must not be forfeited or destroyed during the appeal period unless earlier forfeiture or destruction is permitted by any other law.
This section does not apply to orders made under the Confiscation Act 1997.
Rules of court may provide for securing the safe custody during the appeal period of any property the subject of an order referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Extension of time for filing or serving notice of appeal or notice of application for leave to appeal

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal or, in accordance with the rules of court, the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court at any time may extend the time within which—
a notice of appeal or notice of application for leave to appeal may be filed under this Part; or
a notice referred to in paragraph (a) may be served.
If the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court refuses an application to extend time under subsection (1), the applicant is entitled to have the Court of Appeal determine the application.

nodes.heading: Abandonment of appeal
nodes.text: An appeal to the Court of Appeal may be abandoned in accordance with the rules of court.

nodes.heading: Powers which may be exercised by Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal may exercise the following powers—
to give leave to appeal;
to review a refusal to certify;
to extend the time within which notice of appeal may be filed and served;
to extend the time within which notice of application for leave to appeal may be filed and served;
to grant the appellant bail;
to order stays of sentence;
to call on a court and a respondent to show cause why a question of law should not be reserved for determination by the Court of Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal refuses an application to exercise a power referred to in subsection (1) in relation to any ground of appeal, the applicant is entitled to have the application determined by the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.

An order under section 280(3) or 284A(3) made by the Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal is stayed on the filing of an application to have the application for leave to appeal determined by the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.
An order stayed under subsection (3)—
takes effect on the refusal of the application for leave to appeal by the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal;
is of no effect if the application for leave to appeal is granted by the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Trial judge may be required to provide report on appeal

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court may require a trial judge to provide to the Registrar a report on a case tried by the judge, giving the opinion of the trial judge on the case or on any point arising in the case.
A trial judge must comply with a requirement under subsection (1) in accordance with the rules of court.

nodes.heading: Production of documents, exhibits or other things
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal may order the production of any document, exhibit or other thing connected with the proceeding if the Court of Appeal considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so.

nodes.heading: Order for examination of compellable witness

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, if the Court of Appeal considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so, the Court of Appeal may order any witness who would have been a compellable witness at the trial to attend and be examined before the court, whether or not the witness was called at the trial.

If the Court of Appeal makes an order under subsection (1), it may order that the examination of the witness be conducted, in accordance with the rules of court, before any person appointed by the Court of Appeal for that purpose.
The Court of Appeal may admit as evidence any deposition of a witness taken in an examination under subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Evidence of competent but not compellable witness
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, if the Court of Appeal considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so, the Court of Appeal may receive the evidence of any witness (including the appellant) who is a competent but not compellable witness.
As to competence and compellability of witnesses, see Division 1 of Part 2.1 of Chapter 2 of the Evidence Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Court of Appeal may refer issue or matter for reference determination

nodes.text: This section applies to—
an appeal under this Part or Part 6.4; and
an application for leave to appeal under this Part or Part 6.4.
The Court of Appeal may refer, for the making of a reference determination, any specified issue or matter arising on an appeal or an application for leave to appeal to which this section applies—
to the Trial Division of the Supreme Court constituted by a Judge of the Court within the meaning of the Supreme Court Act 1986; or
to the County Court constituted by a judge within the meaning of the County Court Act 1958.
The Court of Appeal may make any directions it considers appropriate in a referral under subsection (2), including directions about—
the form any reference determination should take; or
procedural matters.
The Trial Division of the Supreme Court or the County Court (as the case requires) to which a referral for a reference determination is made—
must hear and determine the issue or matter in accordance with any directions in the referral; and
may otherwise conduct the hearing and determine the procedure for the hearing as it considers appropriate; and
on the determination of the issue or matter, must provide its reference determinations to the Court of Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal gives leave, the Court of Appeal may hear and determine an appeal against a reference determination as part of the appeal or application for leave to appeal to which the reference determination relates.

Unless the Court of Appeal otherwise determines in accordance with subsection (5), a reference determination is taken to be a determination of the Court of Appeal in the appeal or application for leave to appeal to which the reference determination relates.
A referral under subsection (2) must not be made to—
the Trial Division of the Supreme Court constituted by a Judge of the Court who was also the trial judge in the proceeding which is the subject of the appeal or application for leave to appeal; or
the County Court constituted by a judge who was also the trial judge in the proceeding which is the subject of the appeal or application for leave to appeal.
Nothing in this section limits any powers of the Court of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Reference of question to special commissioner

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal may appoint a special commissioner to inquire into and report on any question referred to the special commissioner by the court if—
the question arises on an appeal under this Part or an application for leave to appeal under this Part; and
the question involves—
prolonged examination of documents or accounts; or
any scientific or local investigation; and
the court considers that the examination or investigation cannot conveniently be conducted before the court; and
the court considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
The Court of Appeal may act on the report of a special commissioner to the extent that the court considers appropriate to adopt the report.
The Court of Appeal may determine the remuneration of a special commissioner.

Subject to subsections (2) and (3), on an appeal under this Part, including an appeal by the DPP, the Court of Appeal must not increase a sentence by reason of any evidence that was not given at the trial or sentencing hearing.
On an appeal under section 291, the Court of Appeal may increase a sentence by reason of evidence of the failure to fulfil an undertaking referred to in section 291(a).

On an appeal under this Part, including an appeal by the DPP, the Court of Appeal may increase a sentence, by reason of any evidence that was not given at the trial or sentencing hearing, if the court considers that—
the originating court was misled at the sentencing hearing as to a material fact; and
an increase in sentence is necessary in the interests of justice.

On an appeal under section 290A, the Court of Appeal may increase a sentence, by reason of any evidence that was not given in the hearing of an appeal under section 254 (an initial appeal), if the court considers that—
the County Court or the Trial Division of the Supreme Court, as the case requires, was misled in the initial appeal as to a material fact; and
an increase in sentence is necessary in the interests of justice.

history.raw: S. 322 amended by No. 48/2012 s. 8 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal may impose a sentence on a person under this Part even though the person does not attend the hearing of an appeal or an application to the Court of Appeal.
The Court of Appeal cannot impose a sentence that requires the consent of the person, for example a community correction order, in the absence of the person.

history.raw: Note to s. 322 amended by No. 65/2011 s. 107(Sch. item 4.6).

nodes.text: For the purposes of this section, the making of an order under section 280(3) or 284A(3) is an imposition of a sentence.

nodes.heading: Bail following appeal
nodes.text: If on an appeal the Court of Appeal orders a new trial or remits a matter to the Trial Division of the Supreme Court or to the County Court, the Court of Appeal may remand the appellant in custody or grant the appellant bail pending the commencement of the new trial or the remitted matter.
Section 277(2) requires the Court of Appeal to order that the appellant appear on a specified date for the new trial.

history.raw: Note to s. 323 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 35.

nodes.heading: Warrants
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal may issue any warrant necessary for enforcing the orders of the court.
In this section—

nodes.heading: ancillary order
nodes.text: means an order (other than the order that is the subject of the appeal) made by the originating court in the proceeding or the County Court or the Trial Division of the Supreme Court on an appeal under section 254, as the case requires.

history.raw: S. 325(1) def. of ancillary order amended by No. 48/2018 s. 38(2).

nodes.text: On an appeal under this Part, the Court of Appeal may set aside or vary an ancillary order, if the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
On an appeal against conviction from the County Court, the Court of Appeal may set aside or vary an order made by the County Court for the suppression of a name.

nodes.heading: Expenses of assessors and special commissioners
nodes.text: Subject to any prescribed rates and scales of payment, the Attorney-General must pay out of money provided by Parliament all expenses of and incidental to—
the appointment of an assessor by the Court of Appeal under section 77 of the Supreme Court Act 1986 in an appeal under this Part;
a reference of a question to a special commissioner under section 320.
Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all criminal proceedings.

nodes.heading: Second or subsequent appeal to Court of Appeal

history.raw: Ch. 6 Pt. 6.4 (Headings and ss 326A– 326M) inserted by No. 44/2019 s. 35.

nodes.heading: Right of second or subsequent appeal against conviction

nodes.text: A person convicted of an indictable offence by an originating court who—
has exhausted the person's right to appeal against conviction under Division 1 of Part 6.3; or
has previously appealed under this Part but leave to appeal was not granted or the appeal was dismissed, in whole or in part—
may appeal to the Court of Appeal against the conviction if the Court of Appeal gives the person leave to appeal.
See the definition of originating court in section 3.
An appeal under subsection (1) may also include an appeal against a conviction for a related summary offence.
An application for leave to appeal under section 326A is commenced by filing a notice of application for leave to appeal in accordance with the rules of court.

The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court must provide to the respondent a copy of the notice of application for leave to appeal within 7 days after the day on which the notice of application is filed.

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave to appeal under section 326A

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal may grant leave to appeal under section 326A if it is satisfied that there is fresh and compelling evidence that should, in the interests of justice, be considered on an appeal.

The Court of Appeal may grant leave to appeal under section 326A against a conviction for a related summary offence only if it grants leave to appeal under subsection (1) in relation to the indictable offence.
In this section, evidence relating to an offence of which a person is convicted is—
fresh if—
it was not adduced at the trial of the offence; and
it could not, even with the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been adduced at the trial; and
compelling if—
it is reliable; and
it is substantial; and
either—
it is highly probative in the context of the issues in dispute at the trial of the offence; or
it would have eliminated or substantially weakened the prosecution case if it had been presented at trial.

Evidence that would be admissible on a second or subsequent appeal is not precluded from being fresh or compelling only because it would not have been admissible in the earlier trial of the offence that resulted in the conviction.

nodes.heading: Determination of second or subsequent appeal against conviction

nodes.text: On an appeal under section 326A, the Court of Appeal must allow the appeal against conviction if it is satisfied that there has been a substantial miscarriage of justice.
In any other case, the Court of Appeal must dismiss an appeal under section 326A.
If the Court of Appeal allows an appeal under section 326A, it must set aside the conviction of the offence (offence A) and must—
order a new trial of offence A; or
enter a judgment of acquittal of offence A; or
if—
the appellant could have been found guilty of some other offence (offence B) instead of offence A; and
the court is satisfied that the jury or, in the case of a plea of guilty to offence A, the trial judge must have been satisfied of facts that prove the appellant was guilty of offence B—
enter a judgment of conviction of offence B and impose a sentence for offence B that is no more severe than the sentence that was imposed for offence A; or

if the appellant could have been found guilty of some other offence (offence B) instead of offence A and the court is not satisfied as required by paragraph (c)(ii), order a new trial for offence B; or

if the court is satisfied that the appellant should have been found not guilty of offence A because of mental impairment, enter a finding of not guilty because of mental impairment and make an order or declaration under section 23 of the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997; or
if the appellant could have been found guilty of some other offence (offence B) instead of offence A and the court is satisfied—
that the jury must have been satisfied of facts that prove the appellant did the acts or made the omissions that constitute offence B; and
that the appellant should have been found not guilty of offence B because of mental impairment—
enter a finding of not guilty of offence B because of mental impairment and make an order or declaration under section 23 of the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997.
If the Court of Appeal orders a new trial, the court must order that the appellant attend on a specified date before the court in which the new trial will be conducted.
Section 326K enables the Court of Appeal to remand the appellant in custody or grant bail pending a new trial.
If the Court of Appeal sets aside the conviction of offence A, it may vary a sentence that—
was imposed for an offence other than offence A at or after the time when the appellant was sentenced for offence A; and
took into account the sentence for offence A.

A power of the Court of Appeal under this section to impose a sentence in substitution for the sentence imposed by the originating court may still be exercised even if the sentence imposed by the originating court is an aggregate sentence of imprisonment.
If at the conclusion of an appeal the appellant remains convicted of more than one offence, the Court of Appeal may either—
impose a separate sentence in respect of each offence; or
impose an aggregate sentence of imprisonment in respect of all offences or any 2 or more offences.

nodes.heading: Stay of sentence and bail pending appeal

nodes.text: If a notice of application for leave to appeal is filed under section 326B, the Court of Appeal may stay a sentence if satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
A prisoner within the meaning of the Corrections Act 1986 who applies for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal under this Part may apply to the Court of Appeal to be granted bail.
On an application under subsection (2), the Court of Appeal may grant the prisoner bail pending the appeal.

nodes.heading: Abandonment of appeal
nodes.text: An appeal under this Part may be abandoned in accordance with the rules of court.

nodes.heading: Powers which may be exercised by Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal may exercise the following powers in this Part—
to give leave to appeal;
to grant the appellant bail;
to order stays of sentence.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal refuses an application to exercise a power referred to in subsection (1) in relation to any ground of appeal, the applicant is entitled to have the application determined by the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Application of sections 316 to 320 and 326
nodes.text: Sections 316 to 320 and 326 apply with any necessary modification to a proceeding under this Part.

nodes.heading: Sentence in absence of offender
nodes.text: The Court of Appeal may impose a sentence on a person under this Part even though the person does not attend the hearing of an appeal or an application to the Court of Appeal.
The Court of Appeal cannot impose a sentence that requires the consent of the person, for example a community correction order, in the absence of the person.

nodes.heading: Bail following appeal
nodes.text: If on an appeal under this Part the Court of Appeal orders a new trial, the Court of Appeal may remand the appellant in custody or grant the appellant bail pending the commencement of the new trial.
Section 326E(2) requires the Court of Appeal to order that the appellant attend on a specified date for the new trial.

nodes.heading: Warrants
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal may issue any warrant necessary for enforcing the orders of the court.
On an appeal under this Part, the Court of Appeal may set aside or vary an ancillary order, if the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
In this section—

nodes.heading: ancillary order
nodes.text: means an order (other than the order that is the subject of the appeal) made by the originating court in the proceeding or by the Court of Appeal on an earlier appeal.

nodes.heading: Reference to Court of Appeal on petition for mercy

nodes.text: If a person convicted on indictment or found unfit to stand trial or found not guilty because of mental impairment petitions for the exercise of His Majesty's mercy in relation to the conviction or finding, or the sentence imposed on the person, the Attorney-General—

history.raw: S. 327(1) amended by No. 25/2023 s. 7(Sch. 1 item 7).

nodes.text: may refer the whole case to the Court of Appeal; or
may refer any point arising in the case to the judges of the Trial Division of the Supreme Court for their opinion.
If the Attorney-General refers the whole case to the Court of Appeal, the Court of Appeal must hear and determine the case as if it were an appeal by the person.

If the Attorney-General refers a question to the judges of the Trial Division of the Supreme Court, those judges or any 3 of them must consider the point and provide the Attorney-General with their opinion.
Nothing in this Chapter affects the prerogative of mercy.
Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all criminal proceedings.

history.raw: Note to s. 327 substituted by No. 68/2009 s. 36.

nodes.text: Clause 11 of Schedule 4 contains transitional provisions.

nodes.heading: Limitations on rules relating to double jeopardy

history.raw: Ch. 7A (Heading and ss 327A– 327S) inserted by No. 81/2011 s. 17.

nodes.text: This Chapter extends to an acquittal in a place outside Victoria if the law of that place permits the acquitted person to be retried.

Subject to subsection (3), this Chapter does not apply if a person is acquitted of the offence charged but is convicted of a lesser offence arising out of the same set of circumstances that gave rise to the charge.
This Chapter applies in the circumstances set out in subsection (2) if the acquittal was tainted.

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Chapter—

nodes.heading: acquittal
nodes.text: includes—
a verdict of not guilty (other than a verdict of not guilty because of mental impairment); and
an entry of not guilty made on the record on the direction of the trial judge; and
a judgment of acquittal entered by the Court of Appeal on an appeal;

nodes.heading: administration of justice offence
nodes.text: means—
perjury or subornation of perjury; or
perverting, or attempting to pervert, the course of justice or conspiracy to pervert the course of justice; or
bribery of a public official, being a judge of the County Court or the Supreme Court; or
a substantially similar offence against the law of a place outside Victoria corresponding to an offence referred to in paragraph (a), (b) or (c).

nodes.heading: Meaning of fresh and compelling evidence

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Chapter, evidence relating to an offence of which a person is acquitted is—
fresh if—
it was not adduced at the trial of the offence; and
it could not, even with the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been adduced at the trial; and
compelling if—
it is reliable; and
it is substantial; and
it is highly probative in the context of the issues in dispute at the trial of the offence.

Evidence that would be admissible on a new trial under this Chapter is not precluded from being fresh or compelling only because it would not have been admissible in the earlier trial of the offence that resulted in the acquittal.

To avoid doubt, a reference in this Chapter to evidence relating to an offence includes a reference to evidence relating to the issue of whether the presumption against criminal responsibility is rebutted in respect of the offence.

nodes.heading: Meaning of tainted acquittal
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Chapter, if at the trial of an offence a person is acquitted of the offence, the acquittal will be tainted if—
the person or another person has been convicted (whether or not in Victoria) of an administration of justice offence in connection with the trial resulting in the acquittal; and
it is more likely than not that, had it not been for the commission of the administration of justice offence, the person would have been convicted of the first mentioned offence at the trial.

nodes.heading: Circumstances in which police may reinvestigate offence after acquittal

nodes.text: In this section—

history.raw: S. 327E(1) def. of senior member substituted as senior police officer No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(a)).

nodes.heading: an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted
nodes.text: includes—

path.definition: an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted

nodes.text: any other offence charged against the person in the same indictment as the charge for the offence of which the person was acquitted; and

path.definition: an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted

nodes.text: any other offence of which the person could have been convicted at the trial of the offence of which the person was acquitted;

path.definition: an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted

history.raw: S. 327E(7)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(e)(ii)).

nodes.heading: reinvestigation
nodes.text: , in relation to an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted, means—
the questioning and search of the person; or
the conduct of a forensic procedure on the person and the taking of the person's fingerprints in accordance with the Crimes Act 1958; or
the search of property or premises owned or occupied by the person and the seizure of any thing found in or on the property or premises, including any vehicle; or
the use of surveillance devices in accordance with the Surveillance Devices Act 1999; or
the doing of anything authorised by a warrant issued under Part 2-5 of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 of the Commonwealth;

nodes.heading: senior police officer
nodes.text: means a police officer of or above the rank of superintendant.

Subject to subsections (5), (6) and (7), a police officer must not conduct, or authorise the conduct of, a reinvestigation of an offence of which a person has previously been acquitted unless the DPP has given written authorisation.

history.raw: S. 327E(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(b)).

nodes.text: Only the Chief Commissioner of Police, a Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant Commissioner may apply to the DPP for an authorisation under subsection (2).
The DPP must not authorise a reinvestigation referred to in subsection (2) unless—
the DPP is satisfied that—
there is, or as a result of the reinvestigation there is likely to be, sufficient new evidence of the commission of the offence by a person to warrant the conduct of the reinvestigation; and
it is in the public interest for the reinvestigation to proceed; and
in the DPP's opinion, the previous acquittal would not be a bar to the trial of the person for an offence that may be charged as a result of the reinvestigation.

A police officer may apply to a senior police officer for written authorisation to conduct, or authorise the conduct of, a reinvestigation referred to in subsection (2) if the applicant reasonably believes that—

history.raw: S. 327E(5) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(c)).

nodes.text: urgent action is required to prevent the reinvestigation being substantially and irrevocably prejudiced; and
it is not reasonably practicable in the circumstances to obtain the DPP's authorisation before taking the action.

On an application under subsection (5), a senior police officer may give written authorisation for a reinvestigation referred to in subsection (2) if the senior police officer reasonably believes that—

history.raw: S. 327E(6) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(d)).

nodes.text: urgent action is required to prevent the reinvestigation being substantially and irrevocably prejudiced; and
it is not reasonably practicable in the circumstances to obtain the DPP's authorisation before taking the action.

A police officer may conduct, or authorise the conduct of, a reinvestigation referred to in subsection (2) without the written authorisation of the DPP or a senior police officer if the police officer reasonably believes that—

history.raw: S. 327E(7) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.6(e)).

nodes.text: urgent action is required to prevent the reinvestigation being substantially and irrevocably prejudiced; and
it is not reasonably practicable in the circumstances to obtain the authorisation of the DPP or a senior police officer before taking the action.
The DPP must be informed as soon as practicable of—
an authorisation given under subsection (6) and the action, if any, taken under the authorisation; or
any action taken under subsection (7)—
and the reinvestigation must not proceed further without the DPP's written authorisation.

The DPP may, by instrument, delegate any function or power of the DPP under this section (other than this power of delegation) to the Chief Crown Prosecutor or a Senior Crown Prosecutor appointed under the Public Prosecutions Act 1994.
The DPP may file a direct indictment (in accordance with Chapter 5) charging an offence the prosecution of which may only proceed if the Court of Appeal gives authorisation under section 327O.
Any circumstances referred to in section 327M(2)—
need not be specified in a charge for an offence referred to in that subsection; and
are not elements of the offence.

nodes.heading: Bail following filing of direct indictment
nodes.text: If an accused is in custody following the filing of a direct indictment under this Chapter, it is to be presumed that the accused is to be released on bail, regardless of the offence charged, pending determination of the DPP's application under section 327H or discontinuance of the prosecution under section 327K.
Sections 331(2) and 411(4) provide further for bail.

nodes.heading: DPP may apply to Court of Appeal

nodes.text: The DPP may apply to the Court of Appeal for an order—
setting aside the previous acquittal of the accused or removing the previous acquittal as a bar to the accused being tried on the direct indictment (as the case requires); and
authorising the continuation of the prosecution of the charge in the indictment.
An application must specify whether it is based on—
a tainted acquittal; or
fresh and compelling evidence; or
an administration of justice offence.
An application based on fresh and compelling evidence cannot be made in relation to an acquittal resulting from a new trial authorised under this Chapter.

An application under subsection (1) is commenced by filing a notice of application in accordance with the rules of court within 28 days after the day on which a direct indictment is filed under section 327F.
A notice of application under subsection (4) must be signed by the DPP personally.
A copy of the notice of application must be served personally on the accused in accordance with section 391 within 7 days after the day on which the notice of application is filed.

The DPP must provide a copy of the notice of application to the legal practitioner who last represented the accused in the criminal proceeding which resulted in the previous acquittal, if that legal practitioner can reasonably be identified.
An accused is entitled to appear at the hearing of an application under this section and may be represented by a legal practitioner.

nodes.heading: Extension of time for filing or serving notice of application

nodes.text: The Court of Appeal or, in accordance with the rules of court, the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court at any time may extend the time within which—
a notice of application under section 327H may be filed; or
a notice referred to in paragraph (a) may be served—
if the court or Registrar considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
The power of the Court of Appeal to extend time under this section may be exercised by the Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal or the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court refuses an application to extend time under subsection (1), the DPP is entitled to have the Court of Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal determine the application.

nodes.heading: DPP may apply only once in relation to particular acquittal
nodes.text: The DPP may make an application to the Court of Appeal under section 327H only once in relation to a particular acquittal.

nodes.heading: DPP must discontinue prosecution if fails to make application
nodes.text: If the DPP fails to make an application under section 327H within 28 days after filing a direct indictment under section 327F, or any extension of that period granted under section 327I, the DPP must discontinue the prosecution (in accordance with Part 5.4) within 14 days after the expiry of the 28 days or the extension (as the case requires).

nodes.heading: Determination of application where acquittal tainted
nodes.text: On an application under section 327H, the Court of Appeal may make any order referred to in section 327O in relation to a person who has been acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied that—
at the time the offence is alleged to have been committed, the offence was punishable by level 4 imprisonment (15 years maximum) or more (however the penalty is described); and
the acquittal was tainted; and
it is likely that a new trial for that offence would be fair, having regard to—
the length of time since the offence is alleged to have been committed; and
whether there has been a failure on the part of the police or the prosecution to act with reasonable diligence or expedition with respect to the making of the application; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.

nodes.heading: Determination of application where fresh and compelling evidence

nodes.text: On an application under section 327H, the Court of Appeal may make any order referred to in section 327O in relation to a person who has been acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied that—
the offence is referred to in subsection (2); and
any circumstances referred to in subsection (2) in respect of the offence were present in the commission of the offence; and
there is fresh and compelling evidence against the person in relation to the offence; and
it is likely that a new trial for that offence would be fair, having regard to—
the length of time since the offence is alleged to have been committed; and
whether there has been a failure on the part of the police or the prosecution to act with reasonable diligence or expedition with respect to the making of the application; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.
Subsection (1) applies to the following offences—
murder;
murder contrary to section 3A of the Crimes Act 1958 (unintentional killing in the course or furtherance of a crime of violence);
conspiracy to commit murder (section 321 of the Crimes Act 1958);
incitement to commit murder (section 321G of the Crimes Act 1958);
attempting to commit murder (section 321M of the Crimes Act 1958);
manslaughter;
workplace manslaughter (section 39G(1) or (2) of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004);
an offence against section 144(1) of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 arising in respect of a contravention of section 39G(1) of that Act;
child homicide (section 5A of the Crimes Act 1958);
homicide by firearm (section 5B of the Crimes Act 1958);
arson causing death (section 197A of the Crimes Act 1958);
trafficking in a drug or drugs of dependence—large commercial quantity (section 71 of the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981);
cultivation of narcotic plants—large commercial quantity (section 72 of the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981);

rape (section 38 of the Crimes Act 1958), rape by compelling sexual penetration (section 39 of the Crimes Act 1958) or armed robbery (section 75A of the Crimes Act 1958) if the offence is committed in circumstances where—
torture (being the deliberate and systematic infliction over a period of time of severe pain on the victim) was involved in the commission of the offence; or
the offender caused really serious injury to the victim; or
the offender threatened to cause death or really serious injury to the victim;
a substantially similar offence against a previous enactment or the law of a place outside Victoria corresponding to an offence referred to in this subsection.

nodes.heading: Determination of application where administration of justice offence
nodes.text: On an application under section 327H, the Court of Appeal may make any order referred to in section 327O in relation to a person who has been acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied that—
at the time the offence is alleged to have been committed, the offence was an indictable offence; and
there is fresh evidence against the acquitted person of the commission of an administration of justice offence in relation to the previous acquittal; and
it is likely that a trial for the administration of justice offence would be fair, having regard to—
the length of time since the administration of justice offence is alleged to have been committed; and
whether there has been a failure on the part of the police or the prosecution to act with reasonable diligence or expedition with respect to the making of the application; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.
On an application under section 327H, if the Court of Appeal is satisfied of the matters in section 327L or 327M, the court may order that—
the previous acquittal of the accused of an offence charged in the direct indictment be set aside or removed as a bar to the accused being tried on the direct indictment (as the case requires); and
the prosecution of the charge in the direct indictment may continue.
On an application under section 327H, if the Court of Appeal is satisfied of the matters in section 327N, the court may order that—

the previous acquittal of the accused be removed as a bar to the accused being tried for the administration of justice offence alleged to have been committed in relation to the previous acquittal; and
the prosecution of the charge in the direct indictment may continue.
In addition to subsections (1) and (2), the Court of Appeal may make any other order that it considers appropriate.
If the Court of Appeal is not satisfied that section 327L, 327M or 327N applies or that a fair trial is likely, the court must order that the charge in the direct indictment is permanently stayed.
If more than one offence is charged in the direct indictment, the Court of Appeal must make an order under subsection (1), (2) or (4) in relation to each charge.
If the Court of Appeal makes an order under subsection (1) or (2), the court may make any order for or in relation to the bail of the accused that the court considers appropriate.

nodes.heading: DPP must elect which offence to prosecute
nodes.text: If the DPP satisfies the Court of Appeal under sections 327L, 327M and 327N, or any 2 of those sections, the DPP must elect to prosecute either—
the administration of justice offence; or
the offence of which the accused has been acquitted or a related offence—
and may proceed only on that basis.

nodes.heading: Amendment of indictment
nodes.text: If the Court of Appeal makes an order under section 327O(1) or (2) in relation to an offence charged in a direct indictment, the trial court must not amend the indictment to significantly change the offence charged.

nodes.heading: Prohibition on making certain references in new trial
nodes.text: At a new trial that has been authorised under this Chapter, the prosecution must not refer to the fact that the Court of Appeal has been satisfied that—
there is fresh evidence, or fresh and compelling evidence, against the accused in relation to the offence charged; or
it is more likely than not that, had it not been for the commission of an administration of justice offence, the accused would have been convicted of the offence charged at the earlier trial.
Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act 1986 permits the court to make an order prohibiting the publication of the whole or part of a proceeding.

nodes.heading: Appeal and review rights unaffected
nodes.text: This Chapter does not affect any right to appeal or review the acquittal of a person.

nodes.heading: Appearance
nodes.text: A party to a criminal proceeding may appear—
personally; or
by a legal practitioner or other person empowered by law to appear for the party; or
in the Magistrates' Court, in the case of an informant who is a police officer or a protective services officer, by a police prosecutor; or

history.raw: S. 328(c) amended by No. 67/2011 s. 3, substituted by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.7).

nodes.text: if the proceeding was commenced by the filing, by a prescribed person or a member of a prescribed class of persons, of a charge-sheet containing a charge for an offence under—
Division 1 of Part 3C or Schedule 3 of the Sentencing Act 1991; or
section 160 of the Fines Reform Act 2014—

history.raw: S. 328(d)(ii) amended by No. 30/2010 s. 77(2), substituted by No. 47/2014 s. 259(a).

nodes.text: by any other prescribed person or any other member of the prescribed class of persons within the meaning of the Sentencing Act 1991 or the Fines Reform Act 2014, as the case requires.

nodes.heading: When accused etc. is required to appear at hearing

nodes.text: An accused must appear at every hearing in the criminal proceeding against the accused, unless otherwise provided by this Act or the rules of court.

A party to an appeal who was the accused in the criminal proceeding to which the appeal relates must appear at every hearing in the appeal, unless otherwise provided by this Act or the rules of court.
The court may excuse a person from appearing at a hearing.
See section 328 for the ways in which an accused may appear.
Division 3 of Part IIA of the Evidence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1958 authorises or requires the appearance of an accused before the court by audio visual link in certain circumstances.

history.raw: Note 2 to s. 329 amended by Nos 69/2009 s. 54(Sch. Pt 2 item 18.2), 38/2016 s. 9(3).

nodes.heading: When accused etc. is required to attend hearing

nodes.text: An accused must attend a hearing in the criminal proceeding against the accused if—
this Act or the rules of court require the attendance of the accused at the hearing; or
the accused has been remanded in custody or granted bail to attend the hearing; or
the court requires the attendance of the accused at the hearing.
A party to an appeal who was the accused in the criminal proceeding to which the appeal relates must attend a hearing in the appeal if—
this Act or the rules of court require the attendance of the party at the hearing; or
the party has been remanded in custody or granted bail to attend the hearing; or
the court requires the attendance of the party at the hearing.
The court may excuse a person from attending a hearing.
If a person fails to attend when required under subsection (1)(a), (1)(b), (2)(a) or (2)(b), the court may issue a warrant to arrest the person.

If a person fails to attend when required under subsection (1)(c) or (2)(c), the court may issue a warrant to arrest the person  if the court is satisfied that the person has had reasonable notice of the requirement to attend.
Section 3 defines attend.

history.raw: Note 1 to s. 330(5) amended by No. 38/2016 s. 9(4).

nodes.text: Section 100(2) provides for the attendance of an accused at hearings in a committal proceeding.
Section 246 provides for the attendance of an accused at hearings conducted under Chapter 5 (Trial on Indictment).
A court may adjourn the hearing of a criminal proceeding before the court—
to any time and place; and
for any purpose; and
on any terms as to costs or otherwise—
that it considers appropriate.
If at any time a court adjourns the hearing of a criminal proceeding, the court may—
allow the accused to go at large; or
remand the accused in custody; or
grant the accused bail or extend his or her bail.
See section 333 of this Act and section 5A of the Bail Act 1977 where the accused is undergoing a sentence of detention in a youth justice centre.

history.raw: Note to s. 331(2) substituted as Notes to s. 331(2) by No. 43/2017 s. 35.

nodes.text: If an order is made under paragraph (a) or (c) and the accused is the subject of a youth remand warrant that was issued in another criminal proceeding, the youth remand warrant remains in effect.

If an accused is remanded into custody under paragraph (b), section 6A(2A) of the Corrections Act 1986 provides that the remand order under paragraph (b) takes effect despite the existence of a youth remand warrant.
If a court has adjourned the hearing of a criminal proceeding to a particular time, it may order that the hearing be held or resumed before that time.
A court may only make an order under subsection (3)—
with the consent of all the parties; or
on the application of a party who has given reasonable notice of the application to the other parties.

If a court adjourns a criminal proceeding in which a jury has been sworn (by jurors taking an oath or making an affirmation), whether or not the accused is present, the court may discharge the jury from giving a verdict and order a new trial.

history.raw: S. 331(5) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.4).

nodes.text: If a court has adjourned the hearing of a criminal proceeding to a particular time and has remanded the accused in custody, the court may order that the accused be brought at any time before then—
before the court; or
to another place specified in the order where facilities exist to enable the accused to appear before the court by audio visual link—
in order that the hearing may be held or continued.
The officer in charge of the prison or youth justice centre or other officer who has custody of the accused must obey an order under subsection (6).

nodes.heading: Transfer of accused between place of detention and court

nodes.text: A person who has the legal custody of an accused in detention must cause the accused to be brought to and from court whenever necessary so that the accused may be tried, sentenced or otherwise dealt with according to law.

If a court considers it in the interests of justice that an accused in detention should be present in court otherwise than for trial, hearing or sentence, the court may order that the accused be brought before the court.
If a court makes an order under subsection (2), the responsible person, on receiving a copy of the order, must cause the accused to be brought before the court in accordance with the order.
See the definitions of in detention and responsible person in section 3.

nodes.heading: Power to return accused to youth justice centre

nodes.text: Despite anything in the Bail Act 1977, if—
the accused in a criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court is undergoing a sentence of detention in a youth justice centre; and
the Magistrates' Court adjourns the proceeding or commits the accused for trial—
the court may, subject to subsection (3), instead of remanding the accused in custody—

direct that the accused be returned to the custody of the Secretary to the Department of Human Services until the end of the sentence of detention or the resumption of the hearing or the commencement of the trial (whichever is the sooner); and
either—
grant the accused bail on a condition that bail is not to be entered until the end of the sentence of detention; or
refuse bail and direct that the accused be brought before the Magistrates' Court at a later date for it to consider the granting of bail.
For the purposes of this section, the end of the sentence of detention means the time when the accused is released from custody, whether on parole or otherwise.
Section 5A of the Bail Act 1977 provides equivalent powers to the Supreme Court and the County Court.

If the Secretary to the Department of Justice and Regulation in a criminal proceeding objects to the accused being returned to a youth justice centre under subsection (1), the court may only order that the accused is to be returned to the youth justice centre if the court has considered—

history.raw: S. 333(3) inserted by No. 43/2017 s. 36(2), amended by No. 3/2018 s. 27.

nodes.text: the antecedents and behaviour of the accused; and
the age and maturity of the accused; and
any evidence of the behaviour of the accused in custody; and
whether an application has been made to the Youth Parole Board regarding the custody of the accused; and
any other relevant factor.
In this section—

nodes.heading: representative
nodes.text: , in relation to a body corporate, means a person duly appointed by the body corporate to represent it for the purpose of doing any act or thing which this section authorises a representative to do.
For the purposes of this section, a representative need not be appointed under the seal of the body corporate.
For the purposes of this section, a statement in writing that—

purports to be signed by a managing director of a body corporate or by any person (by whatever name called) having, or being one of the persons having, the management of the affairs of the body corporate; and
is to the effect that the person named in the statement has been appointed as the representative of the body corporate for the purposes of this section—
is admissible in evidence and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, is proof that the person has been so appointed.
A representative may do any act or thing that a natural person may do in a criminal proceeding subject to the following—
if a body corporate is charged with an indictable offence, a representative may consent to the charge being heard and determined summarily;
if expressly authorised to do so, a representative may plead guilty on behalf of the body corporate;
if expressly authorised to do so, a representative may sign a notice of appeal referred to in section 255 and enter into an undertaking under section 255(5);
if—
a representative appears in a proceeding against a body corporate for an offence; and
a provision of this Act requires something to be done in the presence of the accused, or to be said to the accused—
it is sufficient if that thing is done in the presence of the representative or said to the representative.

nodes.heading: Interpreter
nodes.text: If—
a person is charged with an offence punishable by imprisonment; and
the court is satisfied that the person does not have a knowledge of the English language that is sufficient to enable the person to understand, or participate in, the proceeding—
the court must not hear and determine the proceeding without a competent interpreter interpreting it.

nodes.heading: Subpoenas and witness summonses
nodes.text: A party to a criminal proceeding may apply for the issue of a subpoena in accordance with the rules of court or a witness summons in accordance with the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, as the case requires.

nodes.heading: Victim who is a witness entitled to be present in court

nodes.text: In a criminal proceeding where a victim of the offence is a witness in the proceeding, the court may order the victim to leave the courtroom until required to give evidence only if the court considers it appropriate to do so.

nodes.heading: Court may act on application or on own motion

history.raw: S. 337 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 38 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: Unless the context otherwise requires, a power or discretion conferred on a court by or under this Act may be exercised by the court on the application of a party or on its own motion.

Unless the context otherwise requires, a power or discretion referred to in subsection (1) includes a power or discretion to revoke or vary a decision or order made in the exercise of that power or discretion.

nodes.heading: Court may determine issue in criminal proceeding without oral hearing

nodes.text: In addition to, and without limiting, section 201, a court may determine any issue (other than determining whether an accused is guilty or not guilty) in any criminal proceeding without an oral hearing and entirely on the basis of written submissions and without the appearance of the parties—
if the court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so; and
whether or not the parties consent to the court doing so.
Section 201 provides for issues to be decided before trial on the basis of written submissions and without the appearance of the parties.
For the purposes of subsection (1), in determining whether it is in the interests of justice to determine an issue in a criminal proceeding without an oral hearing, the court must have regard to—
the right of an accused to be present at the accused's trial; and
the right of an accused to a fair hearing; and
the nature of the issue; and
whether the accused or the offender (as the case requires) has had the opportunity to obtain legal advice; and
whether the parties consent to the court doing so.
Nothing in this section affects any other power of the court to determine an issue in a criminal proceeding without an oral hearing.

history.raw: New Ch. 8 Pt 8.2 (Headings and ss 338–389) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
Ch. 8 Pt 8.2 renumbered as Ch. 8 Pt 8.3 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(a).

nodes.heading: Guiding principles
nodes.text: It is the intention of Parliament that in interpreting and applying this Part in any criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence, courts are to have regard to the fact that—

history.raw: New s. 338 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 338 renumbered as s. 390 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(b).

nodes.text: there is a high incidence of sexual violence within society; and

history.raw: S. 338(a) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zw)(i), renumbered as s. 390(a) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(b).

nodes.text: sexual offences are significantly under-reported; and

history.raw: S. 338(b) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zw)(ii), renumbered as s. 390(b) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(b).

nodes.text: a significant number of sexual offences are committed against women, children and other vulnerable persons including persons with a cognitive impairment; and

history.raw: S. 338(c) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zw)(iii), renumbered as s. 390(c) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(b).

nodes.text: offenders are commonly known to their victims; and

history.raw: S. 338(d) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zw)(iv), renumbered as s. 390(d) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(b).

nodes.text: sexual offences often occur in circumstances where there is unlikely to be any physical sign of an offence having occurred.

history.raw: New s. 339 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 339 renumbered as s. 391 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(c).

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence.
This Division applies to all complainants in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

history.raw: S. 339(2)(b) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 49(o), renumbered as s. 391(2)(b) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(c), amended by No. 11/2021 s. 49(1).

nodes.text: This Division applies despite anything in this or any other Act or any rule of law to the contrary.

nodes.heading: Definition
nodes.text: In this Division—

history.raw: New s. 340 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 340 renumbered as s. 392 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).
S. 340(3)(da) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(1), renumbered as s. 392(3)(da) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).
S. 340(4) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(2), renumbered as s. 392(4) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).

nodes.heading: sexual history evidence
nodes.text: means evidence that relates to or tends to establish the fact that the complainant—
was accustomed to engaging in sexual activities; or
had freely agreed to engage in sexual activity (other than that to which the charge relates) with the accused person or another person.

nodes.heading: Prohibition on questions and evidence concerning sexual reputation of complainant
nodes.text: The court must not allow any questions as to, or admit any evidence of, the sexual reputation of the complainant.

history.raw: New s. 341 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 38/2022 s. 73(2).
S. 341 renumbered as s. 393 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(e).

nodes.heading: Restriction on questions and evidence concerning complainant's sexual activities
nodes.text: The complainant must not be cross-examined, and the court must not admit any evidence, as to the sexual activities (whether consensual or non-consensual) of the complainant (other than those to which the charge relates), without the leave of the court.

history.raw: New s. 342 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 342 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 39(4) (ILA s. 39B(1)), renumbered as s. 394 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).
S. 342(ba) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(3), renumbered as s. 394(1)(ba) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).
S. 342(2) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(4), renumbered as s. 394(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of sexual history evidence
nodes.text: Sexual history evidence is not admissible to support an inference that the complainant is the type of person who is more likely to have consented to the sexual activity to which the charge relates.

history.raw: New s. 343 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 343 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zx), renumbered as s. 395 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(g).

nodes.heading: Application for leave
nodes.text: An application for leave under section 342—

history.raw: New s. 344 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 344 renumbered as s. 396 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(h).

nodes.text: in the case of a summary proceeding, must be filed with the Magistrates' Court and served on the informant in accordance with section 392 at least 7 days before the summary hearing;
in the case of a pre-trial cross-examination under an order made under section 198A or a limited preparatory cross-examination under an order made under section 198B, must be—
filed with the County Court or the Supreme Court, as the case requires; and
served on the DPP in accordance with section 392 at least 7 days before the cross-examination;
in the case of a trial, must be filed with the County Court or the Supreme Court (as the case requires) and served on the DPP in accordance with section 392—
at least 14 days before the day on which the trial is listed to commence; or
if a special hearing is to be held, at least 14 days before that hearing;

in the case of a sentencing hearing, must be filed with the relevant court and served on the informant or the DPP (as the case requires) in accordance with section 392 at least 7 days before the sentencing hearing is listed to commence.

nodes.heading: Application for leave out of time
nodes.text: If it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court may hear and determine an application for leave under section 342 after the expiry of the relevant time limit specified in section 344.

history.raw: New s. 345 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 345 renumbered as s. 397 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(i), amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.5).
New s. 346 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 346 renumbered as s. 398 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(j).

nodes.text: An application for leave under section 342 must be in writing and set out the matters required by subsection (2) or (3), as the case requires.
An application for leave to cross-examine the complainant as to the sexual activities of the complainant must set out—
the initial questions sought to be asked of the complainant; and
the scope of the questioning sought to flow from the initial questioning; and
how the evidence sought to be elicited from the questioning has substantial relevance to facts in issue or why it is proper matter for cross-examination as to credit.
An application for leave to admit evidence as to the sexual activities of the complainant must—
identify the evidence that is sought to be admitted; and
set out how the evidence has substantial relevance to facts in issue.

nodes.heading: Waiver of requirement to apply for leave in writing
nodes.text: If it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court may waive the requirement that an application for leave under section 342 be made in writing.

history.raw: New s. 347 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 347 renumbered as s. 399 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(k).

nodes.heading: Hearing of application for leave
nodes.text: An application for leave under section 342 must be heard in the absence of the jury (if any) and, if the accused so requests, in the absence of the complainant.

history.raw: New s. 348 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 348 renumbered as s. 400 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(m).

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave during summary hearing or trial
nodes.text: In the course of a summary hearing or trial, the court must not grant leave under section 342 unless it is satisfied that the evidence has substantial relevance to a fact in issue and that it is in the interests of justice to allow the cross-examination or to admit the evidence, having regard to—

history.raw: New s. 349 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 5/2025 s. 19(2).
S. 349 renumbered as s. 401 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(n).

nodes.text: whether the probative value of the evidence outweighs the distress, humiliation and embarrassment that the complainant may experience as a result of the cross-examination or the admission of the evidence, in view of the age of the complainant and the number and nature of the questions that the complainant is likely to be asked; and
the risk that the evidence may arouse in the jury discriminatory belief or bias, prejudice, sympathy or hostility; and
the need to respect the complainant's personal dignity and privacy; and
the right of the accused to fully answer and defend the charge.
Section 352 limits the relevance of sexual history evidence.

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave during sentencing hearing

history.raw: New s. 350 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 30/2010 s. 65 (ILA s. 39B(1)).
S. 350 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 40 (ILA s. 39B(1)), renumbered as s. 402 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(o).

nodes.text: In the course of a sentencing hearing, the court must not grant leave under section 342 unless it is satisfied that the evidence has substantial relevance to the issue of appropriate sentence and the offender—
has pleaded guilty to all sexual offences charged against the offender; or
has been found guilty of all sexual offences charged against the offender.
In determining, under subsection (1), whether the evidence has substantial relevance to the issue of appropriate sentence, the court must have regard to—

history.raw: S. 350(2) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 40, renumbered as s. 402(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(o), amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.8).

nodes.text: whether the probative value of the evidence outweighs the distress, humiliation and embarrassment that the complainant may experience as a result of the cross-examination or the admission of the evidence, in view of the age of the complainant and the number and nature of the questions that the complainant is likely to be asked; and
the need to respect the complainant's personal dignity and privacy.
Section 352 limits the relevance of sexual history evidence.

nodes.heading: Court must state reasons if leave granted

history.raw: New s. 351 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 351 renumbered as s. 403 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(p).

nodes.text: If the court grants leave under section 342 it—
must state in writing the reasons for granting leave; and
cause those reasons to be entered in the records of the court.
The failure of a court to comply with subsection (1) does not invalidate any order made by it.

nodes.heading: Limitation on sexual history evidence
nodes.text: Sexual history evidence is not to be regarded—

history.raw: New s. 352 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 352 renumbered as s. 404 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(q).

nodes.text: as having a substantial relevance to the facts in issue by virtue of any inferences it may raise as to general disposition; or

as being proper matter for cross-examination as to credit unless, because of special circumstances, it would be likely materially to impair confidence in the reliability of the evidence of the complainant.

history.raw: New s. 353 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 353 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zz), renumbered as s. 405 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(r).

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence.
This Division applies to a protected witness in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Division—

history.raw: New s. 354 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 354 renumbered as s. 406 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(s).

nodes.heading: family member
nodes.text: , in relation to the complainant or the accused, includes—
a person who is or has been married to the complainant or the accused; and
a person who has or has had an intimate personal relationship with the complainant or the accused; and
a person who is or has been the parent or step-parent of the complainant or the accused; and
a child who normally or regularly resides with the complainant or the accused; and
a guardian of the complainant or the accused; and
another person who is or has been ordinarily a member of the household of the complainant or the accused;

nodes.heading: protected witness
nodes.text: means—
the complainant; or
a family member of the complainant; or
a family member of the accused; or
any other witness whom the court declares under section 355 to be a protected witness.

nodes.heading: Court may declare witness to be protected witness
nodes.text: The court may at any time declare a witness to be a protected witness.

history.raw: New s. 355 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 355 renumbered as s. 407 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(t).
Note to s. 355(2) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zza), renumbered as note to s. 407(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(t).

nodes.heading: Protected witness not to be cross-examined by accused in person
nodes.text: A protected witness must not be cross-examined by the accused in person.

history.raw: New s. 356 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 356 renumbered as s. 408 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(u).

nodes.heading: When accused is not legally represented

history.raw: New s. 357 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 357 renumbered as s. 409 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(v).

nodes.text: If the accused is not legally represented, the court must—
inform the accused and the jury (if any) that the accused is not permitted personally to cross-examine a protected witness; and
ask the accused whether the accused has sought legal representation for the cross-examination of a protected witness; and
if satisfied that the accused has not had a reasonable opportunity to obtain legal representation, grant an adjournment if so requested by the accused.

If the accused does not obtain legal representation for the cross-examination of a protected witness (after being given a reasonable opportunity to do so), the court must order Victoria Legal Aid to provide legal representation for the accused for that purpose.
Despite anything in the Legal Aid Act 1978, Victoria Legal Aid must provide legal representation in accordance with an order under subsection (2).
A legal practitioner provided by Victoria Legal Aid must act in the best interests of the accused if the accused does not give any instructions to that legal practitioner.
