Subject to any direction given under section 389E(2)(f), if the accused refuses the legal representation provided under subsection (3), or otherwise refuses to co-operate, the court must warn the accused that the accused will not be permitted to adduce evidence in relation to a fact in issue in order to contradict the evidence of a protected witness unless the evidence on which the accused intends to rely has been put to the protected witness during cross-examination.

nodes.heading: Jury warning concerning legal representation for cross-examination
nodes.text: If the accused is only legally represented for the cross-examination of a protected witness, the trial judge must warn the jury—

history.raw: New s. 358 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 358 renumbered as s. 410 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(w).

nodes.text: that it is routine practice for an unrepresented accused to obtain or be provided with legal representation for the cross-examination of a protected witness; and
that no adverse inference may be drawn against the accused as a result of the cross-examination not being conducted by the accused in person; and
that the evidence given under cross-examination is not to be given any greater or lesser weight as a result of the cross-examination not being conducted by the accused in person.

history.raw: New s. 359 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 359 renumbered as s. 411 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(y).
S. 359(4) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 41, renumbered as s. 411(4) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(y).

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
an offence against section 195N(1) or 195O(1) of the Crimes Act 1958; or
a family violence offence; or

history.raw: S. 359(1)(b) amended by No. 30/2010 s. 66(1), substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 40.

nodes.text: an offence against section 17(1) or 19 of the Summary Offences Act 1966.
This Division applies to all witnesses (including complainants) in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).
This Division applies at any stage of the criminal proceeding, including an appeal or rehearing.

nodes.heading: Alternative arrangements for giving evidence
nodes.text: The court may direct that alternative arrangements be made for the giving of evidence by a witness, including arrangements—

history.raw: New s. 360 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 360 renumbered as s. 412 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(z).

nodes.text: permitting the evidence to be given from a place other than the courtroom by means of closed-circuit television or other facilities that enable communication between that place and the courtroom;
using screens to remove the accused from the direct line of vision of the witness;

permitting a person, chosen by the witness and approved by the court for this purpose, to be beside the witness while the witness is giving evidence, for the purpose of providing emotional support to the witness;
permitting only persons specified by the court to be present while the witness is giving evidence;
requiring legal practitioners not to robe;
requiring legal practitioners to be seated while examining or cross-examining the witness.
Section 337(1) enables this direction to be made by the court on the application of a party or on its own motion.
Section 337(2) provides that this direction may be varied or revoked.

nodes.heading: Evidence given by closed-circuit television or other facilities

history.raw: New s. 362 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 362 renumbered as s. 415 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(a).

nodes.text: This section applies to arrangements referred to in section 360(a) that are directed to be made under that section.
Any place outside the courtroom where the witness is permitted to give evidence is taken to be part of the courtroom while the witness is there for the purpose of giving evidence.
The court must direct that any evidence given by the witness is recorded.

The court may make any order it considers appropriate to enable the witness to view any place or thing, or identify any person or thing, for the purposes of the proceeding or the evidence of the witness.

nodes.heading: When court must direct use of closed-circuit television or other facilities for complainant

history.raw: New s. 363 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by Nos 30/2010 s. 68, 1/2022 s. 124 (ILA s. 39B(1)).
S. 363 renumbered as s. 416 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(b).

nodes.text: If the witness is a complainant in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence, the court must direct that an arrangement referred to in section 360(a) be made unless—
the prosecution applies for the complainant to give evidence in the courtroom; and
the court is satisfied that the complainant—
is aware of the right of the complainant to give evidence in another place by closed-circuit television or other facilities; and
is able and wishes to give evidence in the courtroom.

Subject to subsection (3), if the witness is a complainant in a proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a family violence offence, the court must direct that an arrangement referred to in section 360(a) be made if—

history.raw: S. 363(2) inserted by No. 1/2022 s. 124, amended by No. 5/2025 s. 41.

nodes.text: closed-circuit television or other facilities that enable communication between the courtroom and the other place are available; and
it is practicable to do so.
The court is not required to direct that an arrangement referred to in section 360(a) be made under subsection (2) if—
the prosecution applies for the complainant to give evidence in the courtroom; and
the court is satisfied that the complainant—
is aware of the complainant's right to give evidence in another place by closed-circuit television or other facilities; and
is able and wishes to give evidence in the courtroom.

nodes.heading: When court must direct use of screens for complainant
nodes.text: If the witness is a complainant in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence and is to give evidence in the courtroom, the court must direct that an arrangement referred to in section 360(b) be made unless the court is satisfied that the complainant—

history.raw: New s. 364 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 30/2010 s. 69.
S. 364 renumbered as s. 417 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(c).

nodes.text: is aware of the right of the complainant to give evidence while screens are used to remove the accused from the direct line of vision of the complainant; and
does not wish a screen to be so used.

nodes.heading: When court must direct presence of support person for complainant

history.raw: New s. 365 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 365 renumbered as s. 418 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(d), amended by No. 1/2022 s. 78 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: If the witness is a complainant in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence, the court must direct that an arrangement referred to in section 360(c) be made unless the court is satisfied that the complainant—
is aware of the right of the complainant to have a support person when giving evidence; and
does not wish to have a support person.
Subsection (1) applies whether the witness is to give evidence in the courtroom or in another place.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief of children and cognitively impaired witnesses in sexual offence, assault and family violence matters

history.raw: New s. 366 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 366 renumbered as s. 419 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(e).

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding (other than a committal proceeding) that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—

history.raw: S. 366(1)(c) inserted by No. 48/2012 s. 21(b), amended by No. 42/2015 s. 22, repealed by No. 47/2016 s. 37(10)(b).

nodes.text: a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or

history.raw: S. 366(1)(ab) inserted by No. 19/2017 s. 57, substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 42.

nodes.text: an indictable offence which involves an assault on, or injury or a threat of injury to, a person; or

any offences against section 23 or 24 of the Summary Offences Act 1966 if those offences are related offences to an offence specified in paragraph (a), (ab) or (b), despite whether any such related offences are withdrawn or dismissed before an offence against section 23 or 24 of the Summary Offences Act 1966 is heard and determined.

history.raw: S. 366(1)(d) inserted by No. 48/2012 s. 21(b), amended by No. 5/2018 s. 29.

nodes.text: For committal proceedings see Chapter 4.
This Division applies to a witness in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1) if the witness is—
a person under the age of 18 years; or
a person with a cognitive impairment.
In this Division, witness means a witness referred to in subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief
nodes.text: A witness may give evidence-in-chief (wholly or partly) in the form of an audio or audiovisual recording of the witness answering questions put to him or her by a person prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this section.

history.raw: New s. 367 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 367 renumbered as s. 420 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(f).
S. 367(1)(ea) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 43, renumbered as s. 420(1)(ea) by No. 68/2009 s. 54(f), amended by No. 30/2010 s. 72, substituted by No. 5/2018 s. 30(b), amended by No. 1/2022 s. 12(1).
New s. 368 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (3), a recording referred to in section 367 is admissible as evidence in a summary hearing, special hearing or trial in the proceeding as if its contents were the direct testimony of the witness if—
a transcript of it was served personally on the accused in accordance with section 391, or on the legal practitioner representing the accused in accordance with section 394—
in the case of a summary proceeding, at least 14 days before the contest mention hearing or, if a contest mention hearing is not held, the summary hearing;
in the case of a trial, at least 14 days before the day on which the trial is listed to commence or, if a special hearing is to be held, at least 14 days before that hearing; and

the court is satisfied that the accused and the legal practitioner of the accused were given, in accordance with the regulations, a reasonable opportunity to listen to and, in the case of an audiovisual recording, view the recording; and
at the summary hearing, special hearing or trial, the witness—
identifies himself or herself and attests to the truthfulness of the contents of the recording; and
is available for cross-examination and re-examination.

The admissibility of a recording of the evidence of a person under the age of 18 years is not affected only because the person attains the age of 18 years before the evidence is presented in a proceeding.

The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or any part of the contents of a recording and, if so, the court may direct that the recording be edited or altered to delete any part of it that is inadmissible.
Subject to this section, a recording referred to in section 367 is admissible in evidence as if its contents were the direct testimony of the witness—
in the proceeding; and
unless the relevant court otherwise orders, in—
any new trial of, or appeal from, the proceeding; or
another proceeding in the same court for the charge for an offence specified in section 366(1) or a charge for a related offence; or
a civil proceeding arising from the same facts as those on which the charge for an offence specified in section 366(1) is founded.
The court, by order, may abridge any time fixed—
by or under subsection (1)(a); or
by any order abridging time made under this subsection—
if the court considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so.

nodes.heading: Court may order production of recording made under this Division in certain circumstances

nodes.text: A court may order that a recording referred to in section 367 be produced for use in a proceeding (other than a proceeding referred to in section 368) before that court if the court is satisfied that it is in the best interests of the witness to do so.
If a court makes an order under subsection (1), it must also specify—
the persons who may view or listen to the recording; and
when and where the recording is required to be produced; and
if necessary, any requirements as to the destruction of the recording.
In making an order under subsection (1), the court must have regard to the need to protect the privacy of the witness.
In this section, court includes a tribunal if the complainant is the applicant in a proceeding before the tribunal.

nodes.heading: Procedure and rules for children and cognitively impaired complainants

history.raw: New s. 369 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: This Division applies to a trial in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence.
This Division applies to a complainant in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1) if, at the time at which the proceeding commenced, the complainant—
was under the age of 18 years; or
had a cognitive impairment.
In this Division, complainant means a complainant referred to in subsection (2).

history.raw: S. 369(3) amended by No. 29/2011 s. 3(Sch. 1 item 24).
New s. 370 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (2), the whole of the evidence (including cross-examination and re-examination) of a complainant must be—
given at a special hearing under this Division and recorded as an audiovisual recording; and
in the case of a special hearing before the trial, presented to the court in the form of that recording.
The court must direct that a special hearing under this Division is to be held—
before the trial; or
during the trial.
Section 337 enables the court to vary its direction on the application of a party or on its own motion.
In making a direction under subsection (1A), the court must have regard to—
if the complainant is a child, the age and maturity of the child; and
if the complainant is cognitively impaired, the severity of that impairment; and
any preference expressed by the complainant to give their evidence before the trial or during the trial; and
whether conducting the special hearing during the trial is likely—
to intimidate the complainant when giving his or her evidence; or
to have an adverse effect on the complainant; and
the need to complete the evidence of the complainant expeditiously; and
the likelihood that the evidence given by the complainant will include inadmissible evidence that may result in the discharge of the jury; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.

On the application of the prosecution, the court may direct that subsection (1) is not to apply and that the complainant is to give direct testimony in the proceeding if the court is satisfied that the complainant—
is aware of the right of the complainant to have his or her evidence taken at a special hearing under this Division and audiovisually recorded; and
is able and wishes to give direct testimony in the proceeding.
Division 4 provides that the court may make alternative arrangements for the giving of direct testimony.

history.raw: New s. 371 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50. S. 371(1)(a) amended by No. 5/2025 s. 21(1).

nodes.text: If a special hearing is to be held, it must be held—
within the applicable period after the accused is committed for trial; and
before the court at which the indictment is filed.
Sections 211 and 212 impose time limits for commencing trials for offences.

history.raw: Note to s. 371(1) substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 21(2).

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (1B), the applicable period is—
for a trial in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence, a period of 3 months; or
for a trial in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a family violence offence, a period of 12 months.
If a trial in a criminal proceeding relates partly to a charge for a sexual offence and partly to a charge for a family violence offence, the applicable period is a period of 3 months.
The court may extend the time for holding a special hearing if the court considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so, having regard to—
if the complainant is a child, the age and maturity of the child; and
if the complainant is cognitively impaired, the severity of that impairment; and
the period of time since the complaint was first made; and
the period of time since the offence was allegedly committed; and
any other matter that the court considers relevant.
The court may extend time under subsection (2) before or after the time expires.
More than one extension of time may be granted under subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Timing arrangements for special hearing during trial
nodes.text: If the court directs that a special hearing be held during the trial, the court must—
as far as possible, commence the special hearing on the date specified under section 181(2)(d)(iii); and
ensure that the complainant's evidence is disrupted to the least extent possible.
An application to discharge the jury may be heard and determined after the special hearing is completed.
Sections 211 and 212 impose time limits for commencing trials for offences.

history.raw: Note to s. 371A substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 22.
New s. 372 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: At a special hearing—
the accused and his or her legal practitioner are to be present in the courtroom;
the accused—
is not to be in the same room as the complainant when the complainant's evidence is being taken;
is entitled to see and hear the complainant while the complainant is giving evidence and to have at all times the means of communicating with his or her legal practitioner;
in the case of a special hearing held during the trial, the jury is to be present in the courtroom;
no person, other than a person authorised by the court, is to be present in the courtroom or the same room as the complainant when the complainant's evidence is being taken;

the evidence of the complainant is to be given by means of closed-circuit television or other facilities that enable communication between the room in which the complainant is present and the courtroom;
except as provided by this Division, the usual rules of evidence apply.
The room in which the complainant gives evidence is taken to be part of the courtroom while the complainant is there for the purpose of giving evidence.

nodes.heading: Form in which recording of special hearing is to be tendered

history.raw: New s. 373 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: A recording of a special hearing that is tendered as evidence by the prosecution must be the best available record, or be comprised of the best available records, of the evidence of the complainant.
In subsection (1)— the best available record of the evidence, or any part of the evidence, means an audiovisual recording of the evidence.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced, the court may admit as evidence an audio recording of the evidence, or any part of the evidence, if an audiovisual recording of the evidence is not available.

nodes.heading: Admissibility of evidence from special hearing

history.raw: New s. 374 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: In this section—

nodes.heading: recording
nodes.text: means a recording of a special hearing.
Subject to subsection (3), a recording is admissible in evidence as if its contents were the direct testimony of the complainant—
in the proceeding; and
unless the relevant court otherwise orders, in—
any new trial of, or appeal from, the proceeding; or
another proceeding in the same court for—
the charge for the sexual offence or the family violence offence (as the case requires); or
a charge for a related offence; or
a civil proceeding arising from the same facts as those on which the charge for the sexual offence or the family violence offence is founded.

The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or any part of the contents of a recording and, if so, the court may direct that the recording be edited or altered to delete any part of it that is inadmissible.
A party may apply for a ruling under subsection (3): section 337.
Subject to subsection (3), the whole of a recording must be heard by the court.

The admissibility of a recording of the evidence of a person under the age of 18 years is not affected only because the person attains the age of 18 years before the evidence is presented in a proceeding.

Subject to section 376(3), if under this section a recording is admitted into evidence in a proceeding, the complainant is not required to attend the proceeding unless required to do so for cross-examination or re-examination.

history.raw: New s. 376 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: A complainant whose evidence is recorded under section 370 cannot be cross-examined or re-examined without leave.
A court must not grant leave to cross-examine a complainant referred to in subsection (1) unless the court is satisfied that—
the accused is seeking leave because of becoming aware of a matter of which the accused could not reasonably have been aware at the time of the recording; or
if the complainant were giving direct testimony in the proceeding, the complainant could be recalled, in the interests of justice, to give further evidence; or
it is otherwise in the interests of justice to permit the complainant to be cross-examined or re-examined.
If leave is granted under subsection (2), the complainant must attend the proceeding to be cross-examined or re-examined.

Section 377 previously provided an exception to the hearsay rule in relation to previous representations made by a complainant under 18 years in certain circumstances. This matter is now provided for in section 66 of the Evidence Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Admission of recorded evidence of complainant given in trial for sexual offences

history.raw: New s. 378 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence.
This Division applies to a complainant in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1), other than a complainant whose evidence has been taken at a special hearing under Division 6.
This Division applies to a recording of the evidence (including cross-examination and re-examination) of a complainant given during a trial in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).
If the jury is discharged without verdict before a complainant completes his or her evidence, this Division applies to a recording of the partial evidence of the complainant.
In this Division—

nodes.heading: complainant
nodes.text: means a complainant referred to in subsection (2);

nodes.heading: recording
nodes.text: means a recording referred to in subsection (3) or (4).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of recording of complainant's evidence
nodes.text: Subject to section 381, a recording is admissible in evidence as if its contents were the direct testimony of the complainant—

history.raw: New s. 379 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: in the proceeding; and
unless the relevant court otherwise orders, in—
any new trial of, or appeal from, the proceeding; or
another proceeding in the same court for the charge for a sexual offence or a charge for a related offence; or
a civil proceeding arising from the same facts as those on which the charge for a sexual offence is founded.

nodes.heading: Prosecution to give notice of intention to tender recording

history.raw: New s. 380 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: If the prosecution intends to apply to tender a recording as evidence in a proceeding referred to in section 379, the prosecution must serve on the accused and file in court written notice of that intention at least 21 days before the day on which the trial or hearing is listed to commence.
The court may dispense with or vary a requirement imposed by subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Admission of recording of evidence of complainant

history.raw: New s. 381 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50. S. 381(1AA) inserted by No. 48/2018 s. 32(1).

nodes.text: Subject to this section, the court may admit a recording of the evidence of the complainant.
There is a presumption in favour of admitting the recording.
The presumption in favour of admitting the recording is rebutted if the court considers that it is in the interests of justice that the recording not be admitted, having regard to—
whether the complainant's recorded evidence is complete, including cross-examination and re-examination;
the effect of editing any inadmissible evidence from the recording;
whether the accused would be unfairly disadvantaged by the admission of the recording;
subject to subsection (1A), any other matter that the court considers relevant.
The availability or willingness of the complainant to give further evidence is irrelevant to the question of whether it is in the interests of justice not to admit the recording.
The court may admit the whole or any part of the contents of a recording and may direct that the recording be edited or altered to delete any part of it that is inadmissible.

nodes.heading: Attendance of complainant
nodes.text: Subject to sections 384 and 385, if a recording is admitted into evidence in a proceeding, the complainant is not required to attend the proceeding unless required to do so to give further evidence.

history.raw: New s. 383 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.heading: Direct testimony in addition to recording

history.raw: New s. 384 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: On the application of the prosecution, the court may direct that the complainant is to give direct testimony additional to a recording admitted into evidence if the court is satisfied that—
the complainant is able and wishes to give direct testimony; and
it is in the interests of justice to do so.
A complainant may be cross-examined and re-examined in relation to any direct testimony given by the complainant in response to a direction under subsection (1).
Any other cross-examination requires leave under section 385.

history.raw: New s. 385 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: Subject to section 384(2), if a recording of the evidence of the complainant is admitted into evidence in a proceeding, the complainant cannot be cross-examined or re-examined without leave.
A court must not grant leave to cross-examine a complainant unless the court is satisfied that—
the accused is seeking leave because of becoming aware of a matter of which the accused could not reasonably have been aware at the time of the recording; or
if the complainant were giving direct testimony in the proceeding, the complainant could be recalled, in the interests of justice, to give further evidence; or
it is otherwise in the interests of justice to permit the complainant to be cross-examined or re-examined.
If leave is granted under subsection (2), the complainant must attend the proceeding to be cross-examined or re-examined.

nodes.heading: Form in which recording of complainant's evidence is to be tendered

nodes.text: A recording that is tendered as evidence by the prosecution under this Division must be the best available record, or be comprised of the best available records, of the evidence of the complainant.
In subsection (1)— the best available record of the evidence, or any part of the evidence, means an audiovisual recording of the evidence.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced, the court may admit as evidence an audio recording of the evidence, or any part of the evidence, if an audiovisual recording of the evidence is not available.
In this section—

nodes.heading: hearsay rule
nodes.text: has the same meaning as in the Evidence Act 2008.
The hearsay rule does not prevent—
the admission of a recording in accordance with this Division; or
the use of the recording to prove the existence of a fact that the complainant intended to assert by a representation made in the recorded evidence.

nodes.heading: Admission of recorded evidence of complainant given in summary hearing by Children's Court of certain sexual offences

history.raw: Pt 8.2 Div. 7A (Heading and ss 387A, 387B inserted by No. 28/2016 s. 9.

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—

history.raw: S. 387A(1) amended by No. 28/2016 s. 12, substituted by No. 5/2018 s. 14.

nodes.text: an offence against any of the following provisions of the Crimes Act 1958—
section 38 (rape);
section 39 (rape by compelling sexual penetration);
section 49A (sexual penetration of a child under the age of 12);
section 49B (sexual penetration of a child under the age of 16);
section 49C (sexual penetration of a child aged 16 or 17 under care, supervision or authority);
section 49D (sexual assault of a child under the age of 16);
section 49E (sexual assault of a child aged 16 or 17 under care, supervision or authority);
section 49F (sexual activity in the presence of a child under the age of 16);
section 49G (sexual activity in the presence of a child aged 16 or 17 under care, supervision or authority);
section 49H (causing a child under the age of 16 to be present during sexual activity);
section 49I (causing a child aged 16 or 17 under care, supervision or authority to be present during sexual activity);
section 49J (persistent sexual abuse of a child under the age of 16);
section 50C (sexual penetration of a child or lineal descendant);
section 50D (sexual penetration of a step-child);
section 50E (sexual penetration of a parent, lineal ancestor or step-parent);
section 50F (sexual penetration of a sibling or half-sibling); or
an offence of attempting to commit, or of incitement or conspiracy to commit, an offence referred to in paragraph (a).
This Division applies to a complainant in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

This Division applies to a recording of the evidence (including cross-examination and re-examination) of a complainant given during a summary hearing by the Children's Court in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of recording of complainant's evidence
nodes.text: Division 7 (other than section 378) applies to this Division as if—

history.raw: S. 387B inserted by No. 28/2016 s. 9, amended by No. 37/2017 s. 13(2).

nodes.text: a reference to a sexual offence were a reference to an offence referred to in section 387A(1); and
a reference to a complainant were a reference to a complainant referred to in section 387A(2); and
a reference to a recording were a reference to a recording referred to in section 387A(3); and
a reference to a trial were a reference to a summary hearing of the charge by the Children's Court.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief of complainant in family violence offence proceedings

history.raw: Pt 8.2 Div. 7B (Heading and ss 387C– 387P) inserted by No. 33/2018 s. 116.

nodes.text: In this Division—

nodes.heading: family violence offence
nodes.text: means—
an offence against section 37(2), 37A(2), 123(2), 123A(2) or 125A(1) of the Family Violence Protection Act 2008; or
an offence where the conduct of the accused is family violence within the meaning of that Act;

nodes.heading: recorded statement
nodes.text: means an audiovisual or audio recording of a complainant answering questions put to the complainant by a trained police officer;

nodes.heading: trained police officer
nodes.text: means a police officer who has successfully completed a training course approved by the Chief Commissioner of Police under subsection (2).
The Chief Commissioner of Police may approve one or more training courses for police officers for the purposes of this Division.
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding (including a summary hearing, a committal proceeding and a trial) that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a family violence offence.
Sections 387J and 387K apply to other proceedings.
However, this Division does not apply if the accused was under the age of 18 years at the time the family violence offence is alleged to have been committed.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded statement as complainant's evidence-in-chief

nodes.text: A complainant may give evidence-in-chief (wholly or partly) in the form of a recorded statement in accordance with this Division.
In determining whether or not to have a complainant give evidence wholly or partly in the form of a recorded statement, the prosecution must taken into account—
the wishes of the complainant; and
any evidence of intimidation of the complainant by the accused; and
the purpose of the Family Violence Protection Act 2008.
The purpose of the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is set out in section 1 of that Act.
Subject to this Division, a recorded statement referred to in section 387E is admissible in evidence as if its contents were the direct testimony of the complainant—
in the proceeding; and
unless the relevant court otherwise orders, in any new trial of, or appeal from, the proceeding.
Subject to subsection (4), a recorded statement is admissible under subsection (1) if—
the recorded statement complies with section 387G; and
subject to subsection (3), a copy or transcript of the recorded statement was served in accordance with section 387H; and
subject to subsection (3), the court is satisfied that, if the accused is not represented by a legal practitioner, the accused was given a reasonable opportunity to—
view the recorded statement if it is in the form of an audiovisual recording; or
listen to the recorded statement if it exists only in the form of an audio recording and the accused has not been served with a copy of it; and
at the hearing of the proceeding, the complainant—
identifies himself or herself and attests to the truthfulness of the contents of the recorded statement; and
is available for cross-examination and re-examination.
A recorded statement is admissible under subsection (1) despite non-compliance with subsection (2)(b) or (c) if the parties consent to its use as the complainant's evidence-in-chief.

The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or any part of the content of a recorded statement and, if so, the court may direct that the recorded statement be edited or otherwise altered to delete any part that is inadmissible.
Without limiting what is a reasonable opportunity for the purposes of subsection (2)(c), a reasonable opportunity is taken to have been given if—
the accused was given an opportunity to view or listen to the recorded statement, as referred to in subsection (2)(c), while being questioned in relation to the alleged family violence offence; or
the informant notified the accused in writing that the accused had the right to view or listen to the recorded statement, as referred to in subsection (2)(c), on a day arranged with the informant.
To be admissible as evidence-in-chief under section 387F, a recorded statement—
must be made—
as soon as practicable after the events constituting the alleged family violence offence to which the statement relates occurred; and
with the complainant's informed consent; and
must include, at the end of the recording, an attestation by the complainant as to the truth of the content of the statement; and
subject to subsection (2), must be in the form of an audiovisual recording.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced, the court may admit as evidence-in-chief a recorded statement in the form of an audio recording, if an audiovisual recording of the statement is not available.
A recorded statement is made with informed consent if—
the trained police officer informs the complainant that—
the recorded statement may be used in evidence in a criminal proceeding, a proceeding for a family violence intervention order or, if a court or tribunal orders, another proceeding; and
the complainant may be required to give further evidence in the proceeding, including further evidence-in-chief and evidence on cross-examination and re-examination; and
the complainant may refuse consent to the making of the recorded statement; and
the complainant indicates in the recorded statement that the complainant—
understands the matters referred to in paragraph (a); and
consents to the making of the recorded statement.
If any part of a recorded statement is in a language other than English—
the recorded statement must contain an oral translation of the part into English; or
a separate written English translation of the part must accompany the recorded statement.
A recorded statement must be served on the accused or the accused's legal practitioner in accordance with Part 3.2, Part 4.4 or Part 5.5, as the case requires, subject to the following modifications—

if the accused is represented by a legal practitioner, the legal practitioner must be served with an audiovisual copy of the recorded statement (or an audio copy if the statement is in audio form) but must not give a copy of the recorded statement to the accused or allow the accused to be given, or take a copy of, the recorded statement;
if the accused is not represented by a legal practitioner, the accused must be served with—
an audio copy of the recorded statement (whether the recorded statement is in audio or audiovisual form); or
in the circumstances described in subsection (2), a transcript of the recorded statement.
For the purposes of subsection (1)(b)(ii), an accused is to be served with a transcript rather than an audio copy only if the informant or prosecutor believes that—

serving an audio copy on the accused would be likely to present a reasonably ascertainable risk that the accused would commit an offence under section 387L(1) or (2) in relation to the recorded statement; or
in the particular circumstances of the accused, a transcript is required.
An example for subsection (2)(b) is where an accused is hearing impaired and would not be able to listen to an audio copy of the recorded statement.

In addition to subsection (1), if a recorded statement is to be used in a committal proceeding or a trial on indictment, a transcript of the recorded statement must be served on the accused or the accused's legal practitioner in the same manner as the recorded statement is served under Part 4.4 or Part 5.5, as the case requires.

nodes.heading: Editing or otherwise altering recorded statement
nodes.text: A recorded statement may be edited or otherwise altered only—
with the consent of the parties to the proceeding; or
if editing or altering the statement is required—
so as to avoid disclosure of material that is not required to be disclosed, or must not be disclosed, to the accused; or
to comply with a direction of the court under section 387F(4); or
for the purpose referred to in section 387L(4)(h).
If a recorded statement is edited or altered to avoid the disclosure of material, certain notice requirements may apply— see section 41(1)(f).

nodes.heading: Court or tribunal may order production of recorded statement in certain circumstances

nodes.text: A court or tribunal may order that a recorded statement be produced for use in a proceeding (other than the proceeding in which the statement was used as evidence-in-chief under section 387E or a proceeding referred to in section 387K) before that court or tribunal if the court or tribunal is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
Subsection (1) applies whether or not the proceeding relates to a charge for a family violence offence.
If a court or tribunal makes an order under subsection (1), it must also specify—
the persons who may view or listen to the recording; and
when and where the recording is required to be produced; and
if necessary, any requirements as to the destruction of the recording.
In making an order under subsection (1), the court or tribunal must have regard to the need to protect the privacy of the complainant.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded statement in family violence intervention order proceeding

nodes.text: This section applies if—

an application for a family violence intervention order under the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 arises from the circumstances of the alleged family violence offence in relation to which a recorded statement has been made (whether or not the statement has been used in proceedings referred to in section 387D(1) or whether or not any such proceedings have commenced); or

in a proceeding for a family violence intervention order under the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 an affected family member is the complainant who made a recorded statement and the respondent is the person accused of the family violence offence to which the statement relates (whether or not the statement has been used in proceedings referred to in section 387D(1) or whether or not any such proceedings have commenced).
Without limiting section 65(1) of the Family Violence Protection Act 2008, the recorded statement may be used as evidence in the proceeding for the family violence intervention order.

Section 387L sets out the circumstances in which the respondent may be given, or is not permitted to possess, a copy of the recorded statement and the form in which that statement may be given—see section 387L(3), (4), (5) and (6).
In this section, affected family member, family violence intervention order and respondent have the same meaning as in the Family Violence Protection Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Offences in relation to recorded statements

nodes.text: Unless permitted to do so by this section, a person must not publish a recorded statement.
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum).
Unless permitted to do so by this section, a person, other than the complainant, must not knowingly—
copy a recorded statement; or
supply a recorded statement or a copy of a recorded statement to another person.
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum).
Unless permitted to do so by this section, a person, other than the complainant, must not knowingly possess a recorded statement.
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year maximum).
A person may possess, publish or copy a recorded statement, or supply a recorded statement or a copy of a recorded statement to another person—
for the purpose of investigating the family violence offence to which the recorded statement relates; or

for the purpose of preparing for the proceeding in which the recorded statement is proposed to be used in evidence, including a proceeding for a family violence intervention order referred to in section 387K; or
for the purpose of complying with a court order or tribunal order under section 387J or for preparing for a proceeding to which such an order relates; or
for the purpose of the performance of official functions by—
a member of Victoria Police personnel; or
a member of staff of the Office of Public Prosecutions; or
a judicial officer, member or member of staff of a court or tribunal; or
for the purpose of an investigation or inquest under the Coroners Act 2008; or
for purposes connected with disciplinary action against a police officer under the Victoria Police Act 2013; or
for purposes connected with an investigation into the proper exercise of power by a public official, including an investigation by the Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission; or
for the purpose of training or teaching a prescribed person or testing recording equipment if—
the accused to whom the recorded statement relates has been convicted or found guilty of the charge to which the statement relates; and
all legal proceedings in relation to the subject matter in the recorded statement have been concluded; and

either the complainant consents to the use of the recorded statement for the purpose or the recorded statement is edited or otherwise altered so as to prevent the identification of the complainant and any person referred to in the statement; or
for a purpose, or in the circumstances, prescribed by the regulations.
A person may possess a recorded statement (whether in audiovisual form or audio form) if the statement was—
served on that person in accordance with this Act; or
subject to subsection (6), otherwise lawfully supplied to that person.
Subsection (5)(b) does not apply in relation to—
the supply of a recorded statement in audiovisual form, or a copy of it, to the accused or respondent; or

if the accused or respondent was served only with a transcript of a recorded statement in accordance with section 387H(2), the supply of the recorded statement in audio form, or a copy of it, to the accused or respondent.

For the purposes of Subdivision (1) of Division 1 of Part II of the Crimes Act 1958, the complainant is not involved in the commission of an offence against this section by the accused or respondent, and is not punishable as a principal offender, only because the complainant supplied a recorded statement, or a copy of a recorded statement, to the accused or respondent.
This section does not apply to the publication or supply of a recorded statement as part of the publication or supply of an official court recording of proceedings.
In this section—

nodes.heading: member of Victoria Police personnel
nodes.text: has the same meaning as in the Victoria Police Act 2013;

nodes.heading: prescribed person
nodes.text: means—
a member of Victoria Police personnel other than a protective services officer;
a person or body engaged to provide services to Victoria Police in relation to the installation or maintenance of recording equipment;
a legal practitioner or a person training to become a legal practitioner;
a person, or a person belonging to a class of persons, prescribed for the purposes of this section;
an investigating official (as defined in section 464(2) of the Crimes Act 1958) or a person acting under an investigating official's direction;

nodes.heading: publish
nodes.text: means disseminate or provide access to the public or a section of the public by any means, including by—
publication in a book, newspaper, magazine or other written publication; or
broadcast by radio or television; or
public exhibition; or
broadcast or electronic communication;

nodes.heading: respondent
nodes.text: has the same meaning as in the Family Violence Protection Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Division does not affect other provisions
nodes.text: This Division is in addition to the other provisions of this Part and of the Evidence Act 2008 and does not, unless the contrary intention appears, affect the operation of those provisions or that Act.

nodes.heading: Relationship with Surveillance Devices Act 1999
nodes.text: Despite anything to the contrary in the Surveillance Devices Act 1999, a recorded statement made for the purposes of this Division is not protected information for the purposes of Division 1 of Part 5 of that Act.

nodes.heading: Evidence of specialised knowledge in certain cases
nodes.text: Despite any rule of law to the contrary, in a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual offence, the court may receive evidence of a person's opinion that is based on that person's specialised knowledge (acquired through training, study or experience) of—
the nature of sexual offences; and

the social, psychological and cultural factors that may affect the behaviour of a person who has been the victim, or who alleges that he or she has been the victim, of a sexual offence, including the reasons that may contribute to a delay on the part of the victim to report the offence.

nodes.heading: Audiovisual link evidence from overseas in certain proceedings

nodes.text: This section applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for an offence against—
section 49S(1) of the Crimes Act 1958; or
section 49A(1) of the Crimes Act 1958 as in force before the commencement of section 16 of the Crimes Amendment (Sexual Offences) Act 2016.
The court may, on the application of a party to the criminal proceeding, direct that a witness give evidence by audiovisual link if—
the witness will give the evidence from outside Australia; and
the witness is not an accused in the proceeding; and
the facilities required by subsection (3) are available or can reasonably be made available; and
the court is satisfied that attendance of the witness at the court to give the evidence would—
cause unreasonable expense or inconvenience; or
cause the witness psychological harm or unreasonable distress; or
cause the witness to become so intimidated or distressed that his or her reliability as a witness would be significantly reduced; and
the court is satisfied that it is consistent with the interests of justice that the evidence be taken by audiovisual link.

A witness can give evidence under a direction under this section only if the courtroom or other place in Victoria where the court is sitting (the Victorian point) and the place where the evidence is given (the overseas point) are equipped with audiovisual facilities that—
enable all persons at the Victorian point that the court considers appropriate, to see and hear the witness give the evidence; and
enable all persons at the overseas point that the court considers appropriate, to see and hear appropriate persons at the Victorian point.

The place where a witness gives evidence under a direction under this section is taken to be part of the courtroom or other place in Victoria where the court is sitting while the witness is there for the purpose of giving evidence.
An oath or affirmation to be sworn or made by a witness who is to give evidence under a direction under this section may be administered either—
by means of the audiovisual link, in as nearly as practicable the same way as if the witness were to give the evidence at the courtroom or other place in Victoria where the court is sitting; or
at the direction of, and on behalf of, the court at the place where the witness is to give the evidence by a person authorised by the court.
A court may make any orders that are just for the payment of expenses incurred in connection with the giving of evidence under a direction by the court under this section.

This section does not prevent any other law, or any rule or regulation made under any other law, about taking evidence of a witness outside Australia from applying for the purposes of a proceeding to which this section applies.
Nothing in this section limits the application of this Part to a charge for an offence referred to in subsection (1).

history.raw: Ch. 8 Pt 8.2A (Headings and ss 389A-389K) inserted by No. 5/2018 s. 25.

nodes.text: This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or
an indictable offence which involves an assault on, or injury or a threat of injury to, a person; or

any offences against section 23 or 24 of the Summary Offences Act 1966 if the offences are related offences to an offence specified in paragraph (a) or (c), despite whether any such related offences are withdrawn or dismissed before an offence against section 23 or 24 of the Summary Offences Act 1966 is heard and determined.
This Division applies at any stage of the criminal proceeding, including an appeal or rehearing.
This Division applies to—
a witness (including a complainant) other than the accused in a criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1) if the witness is—
a person under the age of 18 years; or
a person with a cognitive impairment; and
a witness who is a complainant in relation to a charge for a sexual offence.
In this Division, witness means a witness referred to in subsection (3).

nodes.heading: Ground rules hearings
nodes.text: A ground rules hearing is a hearing at which the court—
considers the communication, support or other needs of witnesses; and
decides how the proceeding is to be conducted to fairly and effectively meet those needs.

nodes.heading: Ground rules hearing to be held

nodes.text: The court may direct that a ground rules hearing is to be held.
Section 337(1) enables this direction to be made by the court on the application of a party or on its own motion.
An application for the court to direct that a ground rules hearing is to be held may be made orally or in writing.
A ground rules hearing must be held if—
an intermediary is appointed under Division 2; or
a witness is a complainant in relation to a charge for a sexual offence.

nodes.heading: Time limits for ground rules hearing

nodes.text: If a ground rules hearing is to be held, it must be held before the commencement of any hearing at which a witness is to give evidence.
The court may extend the time for holding a ground rules hearing if the court considers that it is in the interests of justice to do so.
The court may extend time under subsection (2) before or after the time expires.
More than one extension of time may be granted under subsection (2).
The following persons must attend a ground rules hearing—
a person acting for the prosecution;
the legal practitioner representing the accused or, if the accused is unrepresented, the accused;
the intermediary appointed for a witness, if any.
A witness is not required to attend a ground rules hearing.
The court may make an order that a witness for whom an intermediary is appointed not attend a ground rules hearing.

nodes.heading: Directions which may be given at ground rules hearings

nodes.text: At a ground rules hearing, the court may make or vary any direction for the fair and efficient conduct of the proceeding.
Without limiting subsection (1), the court may give one or more of the following directions—
a direction about the manner of questioning a witness;
a direction about the duration of questioning a witness;
a direction about the questions that may or may not be put to a witness;
if there is more than one accused, a direction about the allocation among the accused of the topics about which a witness may be asked;
a direction about the use of models, plans, body maps or similar aids to help communicate a question or an answer;

a direction that if a party intends to lead evidence that contradicts or challenges the evidence of a witness or that otherwise discredits a witness, the party is not obliged to put that evidence in its entirety to the witness in cross-examination.

A direction referred to in subsection (2)(f) may exclude all or part of the operation of the rule attributed to Browne v Dunn (1893) 6 R 67 followed and applied in criminal proceedings in Victoria in R v McDowell [1997] 1 VR 473 (CA), R v MG (2006) 175 A Crim R 342, R v SWC (2007) 175 A Crim R 71 and R v Ferguson (2009) 24 VR 531 in the circumstances in which, and in relation to witnesses to which, this Division applies.

history.raw: Note to s. 389E(2)(f) amended by No. 22/2020 s. 11, repealed by No. 38/2022 s. 72(1).
Notes to s. 389E inserted by No. 38/2022 s. 72(2).

nodes.text: Section 41 of the Evidence Act 2008 requires the court to disallow an improper question or improper questioning put to a witness in cross-examination, or inform the witness that it need not be answered.
This Division applies to a witness (including the complainant) other than the accused in a criminal proceeding if—
the witness—
is under the age of 18 years at the time at which the proceeding commences; or
has a cognitive impairment; and
the criminal proceeding is in a participating venue of a court.
This Division applies at any stage of the criminal proceeding, including an appeal or rehearing.
In this Division (other than in section 389J(4)(c)), witness means a witness referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Participating venues of courts
nodes.text: The Minister may, by notice published in the Government Gazette, declare a venue of a court to be a participating venue for the purposes of this Division.
The Secretary to the Department of Justice and Regulation must establish a panel of persons who the Secretary is satisfied are suitable persons to be appointed as intermediaries.
A person must not be on the panel unless the person—
has a tertiary qualification in psychology, social work, speech pathology or occupational therapy; or
has other prescribed qualifications, training, experience or skills.

The Secretary to the Department of Justice and Regulation must remove a person from the panel if the Secretary is no longer satisfied that the person is a suitable person to be appointed as an intermediary.
The function of an intermediary is—
to communicate or explain to a witness for whom an intermediary is appointed, questions put to the witness to the extent necessary to enable them to be understood by the witness; and

to communicate or explain to a person asking questions of a witness for whom an intermediary is appointed, the answers given by the witness in reply to the extent necessary to enable them to be understood by the person.
An intermediary is an officer of the court and has a duty to act impartially when assisting communication with the witness.
A court may appoint an intermediary for a witness from the panel established under this Division.
Section 337(1) enables this appointment to be made by the court on the application of a party or on its own motion.
Section 337(2) provides that this appointment may be varied or revoked.
An application for a court to appoint an intermediary may be made orally or in writing.
A court must not appoint an intermediary for a witness if the court is satisfied that the witness—
is aware of the right of the witness to make an application for an intermediary to be appointed; and
is able and wishes to give evidence in the criminal proceeding without the assistance of an intermediary.
A court must not appoint a person as an intermediary for a witness if the person—
is a relative, friend or acquaintance of the witness or the accused; or
has assisted the witness (other than as an intermediary) or the accused in a professional capacity; or
is a party or potential witness (other than by reason of the person's role as an intermediary) in the relevant proceeding.

nodes.heading: Witness to give evidence in presence of intermediary

nodes.text: In a proceeding in which an intermediary has been appointed, the evidence of the witness must be given in the presence of the intermediary.
Subject to any direction of the court and rules of court, the evidence of the witness given in the presence of the intermediary must be given in circumstances in which—
the court and any legal practitioner appearing in the proceeding are able to see and hear the witness giving evidence and to communicate with the intermediary; and

the jury (if any) is able to see and hear the witness giving evidence (including any assistance given by the intermediary), other than evidence given in accordance with an arrangement made under section 360(a) as directed by the court.
The provisions of Division 2 (other than section 22(2)) of Part 2.1 of the Evidence Act 2008 which apply to interpreters are taken to apply to an intermediary.
Section 22(2) of the Evidence Act 2008 requires interpreters to take an oath or make an affirmation in accordance with a form in Schedule 1 to that Act or a similar form.
A person must not act as an intermediary in a particular proceeding unless the person has taken an oath or made an affirmation in the prescribed form.

history.raw: Ch. 8 Pt 8.3 renumbered as Ch. 8 Pt 8.4 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(l).

nodes.heading: General rules as to service
nodes.text: Unless this Act or any other Act or the rules of court otherwise provide—
if a document is to be served personally, it must be served in accordance with section 391;
if a document is to be served on the informant or the prosecution, it must be served in accordance with section 392;
if a document is to be served on a company, registered body, incorporated association or other body corporate, it must be served in accordance with section 393;
in any other case, a document may be served in accordance with section 394.
Unless this Act or any other Act or the rules of court otherwise provide, personal service of a document must be effected in accordance with subsection (2), (3) or (4).
Personal service of a document is effected by—
giving a copy of the document to the person to be served; or
putting the copy down in the person's presence and telling the person the nature of the document; or
leaving a copy of the document for the person at the person's last known or usual place of residence with a person who appears to be of or over the age of 16 years.

For the purposes of subsection (2)(c), a person satisfies the requirement to leave a copy of a document with another person by putting a copy of the document down in the presence of the other person and telling the person the nature of the document.

If the person to be served is in detention or in immigration detention within the meaning of section 5 of the Migration Act 1958 of the Commonwealth, personal service of a document on the person may be effected by  sending a copy of the document by registered post addressed to the person at the place of detention.
See the definition of in detention in section 3.

If a legal practitioner has given written notice to the informant or the prosecution that the legal practitioner represents an accused and is instructed to accept personal service of documents on behalf of the accused, personal service of a document on the accused may be effected by—
giving a copy of the document to the legal practitioner; or
leaving a copy of the document at the ordinary place of business of the legal practitioner with a person who appears to work there; or
sending a copy of the document by registered post addressed to the legal practitioner at the ordinary business address of the legal practitioner; or
delivering a copy of the document by means of fax or email to the legal practitioner of the person who—
has consented to receiving documents on the person's behalf by fax or email; and
has provided a fax number or address or email address to the prosecution or informant in the matter in respect of which the legal practitioner is representing the person; or
if the legal practitioner—
has facilities for the reception of documents in a document exchange; and
consents to accepting personal service of documents by delivery to those facilities in the document exchange—
by delivering a copy of the document addressed to the legal practitioner into those facilities.
If a document is delivered into the facilities of a document exchange in accordance with subsection (4)(d), the day of service of the document is taken to be—
the day following the day on which it is so delivered; or
if the document is delivered on a Friday, the following Monday—
or on any other day that may be proved.
In this section—

nodes.heading: informant
nodes.text: includes an appellant, applicant or respondent who was the informant at first instance.
If the person to be served is the informant, a document may be served—
by giving a copy of the document to—
the informant; or
a person representing the informant at a hearing in relation to the charge; or
by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the informant at the business address nominated by the informant under section 18; or
by sending a copy of the document by fax or email addressed to the informant at the fax number or email address nominated by the informant under section 18; or
by leaving a copy of the document for the informant at the informant's business address nominated under section 18 with a person who appears to work there; or
in any other manner agreed between the informant and the party serving the document.
If the person to be served is the DPP, a document may be served—
by giving a copy of the document to a person representing the DPP at a hearing in relation to the charge; or
by leaving a copy of the document at the Office of Public Prosecutions with a person who appears to work there; or
by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the Office of Public Prosecutions at the ordinary business address of the Office of Public Prosecutions; or
by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the DPP at the business address, if any, nominated by the DPP under section 172; or
if the DPP has facilities for the reception of documents in a document exchange, by delivering a copy of the document addressed to the DPP into those facilities; or
by sending a copy of the document by fax or email addressed to the DPP at the fax number or email address, if any, nominated by the DPP under section 172; or
in any other manner agreed between the DPP and the party serving the document.
If a document is delivered into the facilities of a document exchange in accordance with subsection (3)(da), the day of service of the document is taken to be—
the day following the day on which it is so delivered; or
if the document is delivered on a Friday, the following Monday—
or on any other day that may be proved.
The Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 applies to enable a document to be served electronically, including facsimile transmission and email, in accordance with that Act.
Section 172 provides that the DPP may nominate an address for service of documents.

nodes.heading: Service on company, registered body, incorporated association or other body corporate

nodes.text: If the person to be served is a company within the meaning of the Corporations Act, service of a document on the person may be effected in accordance with section 109X of that Act or in accordance with subsection (4).

If the person to be served is a registered body within the meaning of the Corporations Act, service of a document on the person may be effected in accordance with section 601CX of that Act or in accordance with subsection (4).

If the person to be served is an incorporated association within the meaning of the Associations Incorporation Reform Act 2012, service of a document on the person may be effected in accordance with section 217 of that Act or in accordance with subsection (4).
If the person to be served is a body corporate and service is not effected in accordance with subsection (1), (2) or (3), service of a document on the person must be effected—
by leaving a copy of the document at the registered office or principal place of business of the body corporate; or
by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post to the registered office or principal place of business of the body corporate; or

if the body corporate is represented by a legal practitioner, by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the legal practitioner at the ordinary business address of the legal practitioner; or
by serving a copy of the document on a representative of the body corporate within the meaning of section 334 in a manner nominated in writing by the representative.

The Electronic Transactions Act 1999 of the Commonwealth or the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 applies to enable a document to be served electronically, including fax transmission and email, in accordance with the relevant Act.
Unless this Act or any other Act or the rules of court otherwise provide, ordinary service of a document is effected—
by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the person to be served at the last known place of residence or business of the person; or

if the document relates only to a traffic camera offence, by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the person to be served at a post office box address nominated by the person; or

if the person to be served is represented by a legal practitioner, by sending a copy of the document by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the legal practitioner at the ordinary business address of the legal practitioner; or

if the person to be served is represented by a legal practitioner who has facilities for the reception of documents in a document exchange, by delivering a copy of the document addressed to the legal practitioner into those facilities; or
in any other manner agreed by the parties.
See section 49 of the Interpretation of Legislation Act 1984 as to service by post.
The Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 applies to enable a document to be served electronically, including fax transmission and email, in accordance with that Act.
If a document is delivered into the facilities of a document exchange in accordance with subsection (1)(ba), the day of service of the document is taken to be—
the day following the day on which it is so delivered; or
if the document is delivered on a Friday, the following Monday—
or on any other day that may be proved.

nodes.heading: Personal service satisfies ordinary service
nodes.text: If this Act requires or permits service of a document to be effected in accordance with section 394 or by ordinary service, the document may be served in accordance with section 391.

nodes.heading: Last known place of residence or business
nodes.text: Rules of court may prescribe how the last known place of residence or business of an accused is to be ascertained in specified circumstances.

nodes.heading: Order for substituted service
nodes.text: If it appears to a court by sworn or affirmed evidence, whether oral or by affidavit, that service cannot be promptly effected, the court may make an order for substituted service.

nodes.heading: Who may effect service
nodes.text: If by or under this Act a person is required or permitted to serve a document, the person may serve the document by causing it to be served by another person.
Service of a document may be proved by—
oral sworn or affirmed evidence; or

history.raw: S. 399(1)(a) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.6(a)).

nodes.text: affidavit; or
statutory declaration.

history.raw: S. 399(1)(c) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.6(b)).

nodes.text: Evidence of service must identify the document served and state the time and manner in which service was effected.

A document purporting to be an affidavit or statutory declaration under subsection (1)(b) or (1)(c) is admissible in evidence and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, is proof of the statements in it.

history.raw: S. 399(3) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.6(b)).

nodes.text: An affidavit or statutory declaration under subsection (1)(b) or (1)(c) must be filed in court—

history.raw: S. 399(4) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.6(b)).

nodes.text: in the case of service of a summons to answer to a charge for an indictable offence where a date for a filing hearing has been fixed, at least 2 days before the filing hearing;
in the case of service of any other summons to answer to a charge, at least 7 days before the return date;
in the case of service of any other document, a reasonable time before the hearing to which it applies.

history.raw: Ch. 8 Pt 8.4 renumbered as Ch. 8 Pt 8.5 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(x). S. 410A inserted by No. 31/2024 s. 10.

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (2), the court must not make an order awarding costs against a person without giving that person a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
Subsection (1) does not apply to an order for costs made on the hearing and determination of a charge in the absence of the accused in accordance with Division 10 of Part 3.3.

nodes.heading: Costs in summary proceedings and committal proceedings

nodes.text: Unless otherwise expressly provided by this or any other Act or by the rules of court, the costs of, and incidental to, all criminal proceedings in the Magistrates' Court are in the discretion of the court and the court has full power to determine by whom, to whom and to what extent the costs are to be paid.

In exercising its discretion under subsection (1) in a criminal proceeding, the Magistrates' Court may take into account any unreasonable act or omission by, or on behalf of, a party to the proceeding that the court is satisfied resulted in prolonging the proceeding.
If the Magistrates' Court strikes out a charge under section 14(3), the court may award costs against the informant.
This section and section 410 apply to a purported proceeding in the Magistrates' Court which is beyond the jurisdiction of the court as if the purported proceeding were within jurisdiction.
If the Magistrates' Court determines to award costs against an informant who is a police officer, the order must be made against the Chief Commissioner of Police.

history.raw: S. 401(5) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.8).

nodes.text: If a notice to appear lapses under section 22(1) and notice is given in accordance with section 23, the police officer or public official who served the notice is not liable for any costs of the person served with the notice in respect of the serving or lapsing of the notice.

history.raw: S. 402(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.8).

nodes.text: If a notice to appear lapses under section 22(1) and notice is not given in accordance with section 23, the Magistrates' Court may award costs against the police officer or public official who served the notice as if the notice to appear were a criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court.

nodes.heading: Convicted accused to pay filing fee
nodes.text: If—
a charge-sheet containing one or more charges is filed with a registrar of the Magistrates' Court; and
no filing fee is payable because of an exemption provided for in the regulations; and
the accused is convicted of one or more of the alleged offences and is ordered to pay a fine—

the Magistrates' Court must order the accused to pay by way of costs, in addition to the amount of the fine and any other costs, the amount of the filing fee that, but for the exemption, would have been payable.

nodes.heading: Costs in the Supreme Court and County Court

nodes.text: If—
the Supreme Court or the County Court is satisfied that an act or omission by, or on behalf of, a party before the commencement of trial was unreasonable and resulted in prolonging the trial; or
there has been a departure referred to in section 233; or

history.raw: S. 404(2)(b) amended by No. 17/2014 s. 160(Sch. 2 item 30.3).

nodes.text: a party has failed to comply with a requirement of Part 5.5 or an order made under that Part—

the court may make any order that it considers appropriate with respect to the costs of and incidental to the trial and, for this purpose, it has full power to determine by whom, to whom and to what extent those costs are to be paid.
An order under subsection (1) may be made against—
a party, whether the Crown or the accused; or
a party's legal practitioner or, in the case of a legal practitioner who is employed by a law practice (within the meaning of the Legal Profession Uniform Law (Victoria)), the law practice.
If the accused and the accused's legal practitioner have complied with the requirements of Part 5.5 and any orders made under that Part and the hearing of a criminal proceeding is—
discontinued or adjourned; and
the reason for the discontinuance or the adjournment was not attributable in any way to the act, neglect or fault of an accused or that accused's legal practitioner—

any indemnity certificate granted by the court under section 16 or 17 of the Appeal Costs Act 1998 may include an indemnity certificate for the accused's own costs incurred in consequence of a requirement imposed on the accused under that Part.

nodes.heading: Costs order
nodes.text: If the court determines that costs should be paid under section 404 or 410, the order must provide—

if the court is satisfied that a party or a party's legal practitioner has reasonably incurred additional costs as a consequence of any act or omission of another party, for payment of costs to the first-mentioned party or that party's legal practitioner;
in any other case, for payment of costs into court for payment into the Consolidated Fund.

nodes.heading: Costs on appeal to County Court or the Court of Appeal under section 254

history.raw: S. 406 (Heading) amended by Nos 3/2016 s. 83(1), 1/2022 s. 76(1).

nodes.text: If—
an appeal under section 254 is struck out or dismissed; and
the County Court or the Court of Appeal, as the case requires, is satisfied that the appeal was brought vexatiously or frivolously or in abuse of process—
the court may order that the appellant pay all or a specified portion of the respondent's costs of the appeal.

Nothing in subsection (1) limits any discretion as to costs of an appeal conferred on the County Court or the Supreme Court, as the case requires, by any other provision of this Act or the County Court Act 1958 or the Supreme Court Act 1986, as the case requires.
If the County Court or the Supreme Court, as the case requires, is satisfied that—
a copy of a notice of appeal under section 254 or 257 was served on the respondent; and
the appeal was not afterwards prosecuted or the court has no jurisdiction to hear and determine the appeal—
the court may order that the appellant pay to the respondent any costs that it thinks reasonable.
If an appellant under section 254—
breaches an undertaking referred to in section 255(5); or
abandons an appeal—
the court may order that the appellant pay any costs incurred as a result of the breach or abandonment.

nodes.heading: Costs on abandonment of appeal to County Court or the Court of Appeal

history.raw: S. 407 (Heading) amended by Nos 3/2016 s. 84(1), 1/2022 s. 77(1).

nodes.text: Within 28 days after receiving a copy of the order striking out an appeal, the respondent may apply to the County Court or the Court of Appeal, as the case requires, for an order dealing with the respondent's costs of the appeal.
If a respondent proposes to apply to the court under subsection (1), the respondent must first serve notice in writing of the proposed application on the appellant.
See section 394 for ordinary service.
On an application under subsection (1), the court may make any order that it considers just.

nodes.heading: Costs on appeal from Magistrates' Court to Supreme Court on a question of law
nodes.text: The costs of, and incidental to, an appeal under section 272 are in the discretion of the Supreme Court and the court has full power to determine by whom and to what extent the costs are to be paid.

nodes.heading: No costs on appeal to Court of Appeal or on new trial
nodes.text: No costs are to be allowed to a party to—
an appeal under Part 6.3 or 6.4; or
a new trial; or
a proceeding preliminary or incidental to an appeal or new trial.
If a legal practitioner for a party to—
a criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court; or
a criminal proceeding in the Supreme Court or the County Court before the commencement of trial—

whether personally or through a servant or agent, has caused costs to be incurred improperly or without reasonable cause or to be wasted by undue delay or negligence or by any other misconduct or default, the court may make an order that—
all or any of the costs between the legal practitioner and the client be disallowed or that the legal practitioner repay to the client the whole or part of any money paid on account of costs; or
the legal practitioner pay to the client all or any of the costs which the client has been ordered to pay to any party; or
the legal practitioner pay all or any of the costs payable by any party other than the client.
